#9959. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9958. What Is Futures Earn and How Does It Work for Traders?

MEXC Learn is an educational platform that helps users understand crypto trading, blockchain basics, and Web3 concepts.

MEXC Learn is an educational platform that helps users understand crypto trading, blockchain basics, and Web3 concepts.

MEXC Learn is an educational platform that helps users understand crypto trading, blockchain basics, and Web3 concepts.

Futures traders often keep spare stablecoins in their accounts for margin and new entries, and those funds may not earn interest. Futures Earn may allow eligible balances to accrue interest without leaving the account, while those funds remain available for trading.

Quick answer: Futures Earn is an exchange feature that pays interest on eligible balances in a futures account while the funds stay available for trading. Actual earnings depend on the APR, eligible principal, minimum balance requirements, principal caps, and platform-specific conditions.

Futures Earn is an interest product built into the futures account. Once switched on, supported assets in that account, usually stablecoins such as USDT, earn interest automatically. Depending on the platform, qualifying funds may stay in the futures account rather than being locked in a separate savings product, allowing them to remain available for trading.

Keep the two income streams apart: interest comes from holding an eligible balance, while trading profit or loss comes from your positions. You can earn interest while your trades lose money, and it will not cover those losses.

Supported assets, rates, and eligibility rules vary by exchange.

The amount that earns interest is the interest-bearing principal, which is not always your full balance. Some platforms determine eligible principal using balance snapshots, so it can differ from your real-time balance.

Some programs require a minimum balance and set principal caps above which additional funds earn nothing. Base interest and bonus interest may also have different caps.

APR (annual percentage rate) is an annualized rate; the examples below use simple interest without assuming compounding. Unlike APR, annual percentage yield (APY) accounts for compounding.

The base APR may apply without an open position, while qualifying positions can unlock a bonus APR.

For example, MEXC's futures earn program combines interest on eligible futures balances with potential position-based bonuses. The applicable rate depends on the account's eligibility and product conditions.

A higher advertised APR does not necessarily mean higher earnings. Position requirements, principal caps, and the length of time funds remain eligible can all affect the actual payout.

Some exchanges take balance and position snapshots, check eligibility, then calculate interest.

The calculation frequency and distribution schedule depend on the platform. Some products calculate interest hourly and credit it daily, while others follow different settlement rules.

Withdrawals, smaller positions, or lower eligible balances can reduce future earnings.

A simple estimate uses this formula when the same principal qualifies for the full APR:

Estimated Daily Interest = Eligible Principal × APR ÷ 365

For example, assume 10,000 USDT of eligible principal at 5% APR:

However, base and bonus interest may apply to different principal amounts. A more precise estimate is:

Estimated Daily Interest = [(Base Principal × Base APR) + (Bonus Principal × Bonus APR)] ÷ 365

Here, bonus APR means the additional rate, not the combined total.

Suppose 10,000 USDT qualifies for 5% base APR, but only 2,000 USDT qualifies for an additional 15% APR. Estimated daily interest would be:

[(10,000 × 5%) + (2,000 × 15%)] ÷ 365 ≈ 2.19 USDT

These are illustrative calculations, not quotes for a specific account. They assume unchanged principal and rates throughout the calculation period. Actual payouts depend on applicable caps, qualifying periods, balance snapshots, and settlement rules.

MEXC Futures Auto-Earn lets eligible users earn interest while trading futures, with qualifying balances remaining available as margin.

The November 2026 upgrade highlights USDT and USDE. Users should check the rates and conditions displayed in their own accounts before activating the feature.

Log in to your MEXC account and open Futures Earn from the Earn menu.

Check supported assets, minimum balances, personalized APRs, principal caps, and bonus tiers.

MEXC's November 3, 2026 USDT offer advertises a 5% base APR for eligible balances of at least 100 USDT, plus these position-based bonuses:

●       1,000 USDT position value: +1% APR

The highest tier brings the advertised total to 20% APR. However, MEXC's June 8 update introduced personalized APRs and separate principal caps for base and bonus interest. Actual account rates may differ.

The November 2026 USDE offer also advertises a 4.75% base APR.

Position value determines your bonus tier, not your interest-bearing principal. Holding 5,000 USDT while maintaining a 100,000 USDT qualifying position does not mean 100,000 USDT earns interest.

MEXC determines qualifying exposure using net futures position values averaged across snapshots. Coin-M Futures, USDCUSDT, Copy Trading, Grid Trading, Event Futures, and sub-account positions are excluded under its published FAQ.

Users must meet Primary KYC and regional eligibility requirements. Certain restricted regions, account types, or compliance conditions may prevent participation.

#9957. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9955. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

The idea of leasing out address space tied to a government block is fascinating, but the real worry is how much trust downstream networks place in who announces a prefix. If BGP origin validation is not airtight, a rented slice with a White House label is a gift to anyone doing phishing or traffic hijacks.

What struck me is how mundane the mechanism is: a staffer installs a free app, and suddenly a government IP becomes rentable inventory. Egress filtering and device policy on staff phones seem like a far cheaper fix than anything fancy at the routing layer.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.

#9954. 5 Banking Compliance Risks Every Independent Contractor Needs to Understand

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Suppose you just closed the best quarter of your independent career. You signed three new international clients, doubled your monthly billings, set aside your quarterly tax estimate, and finally have enough surplus cash to move a healthy chunk into your brokerage account. From where you sit, you are the exact kind of upwardly mobile customer any financial institution should roll out the red carpet to keep.

Inside the bank’s automated risk engine, that exact same month looks like a four-alarm fire. After 25 years working inside traditional retail and commercial banking, I have sat in the compliance review meetings where accounts like yours land on the chopping block. When the bank’s Transaction Monitoring System (TMS) scans your ledger at two in the morning, it does not see your GitHub commits, your pitch decks, or the late-night Zoom calls behind your invoices. It sees a sudden spike in cross-border velocity, wires arriving from three unrelated corporate entities in different jurisdictions, and rapid outbound transfers to external investment or fintech platforms. In compliance shorthand, your breakout quarter reads like textbook layering or unlicensed commercial activity running through a retail checking account.

Traditional consumer banking infrastructure was built for a 20th-century economic citizen. The entire retail model assumes one local employer, one predictable domestic payroll deposit hitting on the 1st and the 15th of every month, and predictable local debit card spending on groceries, utilities, and a domestic mortgage. Today, millions of legitimate software engineers, independent consultants, indie founders, and remote contractors earn clean global income, yet their banks routinely freeze their balances, hold incoming wires in review queues, demand invasive documentation, or reject their mortgage applications outright.

Banks do not punish self-employed people and remote workers out of personal malice. They punish them because of brutal compliance unit economics and rigid statistical risk modeling. Once you understand how those internal calculators work, you can stop taking account reviews personally and start structuring your finances to reduce avoidable false positives and survive routine compliance checks intact.

A standalone personal checking account is frequently a money-loser for a commercial bank unless you carry a substantial, idle cash balance or borrow money at high interest rates. Banks earn retail margins on the net interest spread (taking your low-cost deposits and lending them out) and on interchange fees when you swipe your card. According to StrategyCorps’ retail checking performance benchmarks, roughly 40 percent of all retail checking relationships are unprofitable for the institution holding them. In its analysis of nearly four million consumer checking relationships drawing on research from groups including the American Bankers Association (ABA) and the FDIC, StrategyCorps notes that maintaining and servicing a checking account costs a bank an estimated USD 250 to USD 400 per year, meaning accounts generating less than USD 350 in annual fee and net interest revenue fail to cover their baseline operating overhead. When a remote worker receives a large payment and immediately sweeps most of it into an external treasury bill account, a multi-currency fintech app, or an index fund, the bank absorbs all the regulatory liability of clearing the payment without keeping the deposit long enough to earn meaningful net interest income on it.

Meanwhile, missing a single bad actor can be catastrophic. Look at what happened when FinCEN assessed a record USD 1.3 billion penalty against TD Bank after regulators found that its monitoring systems failed to catch illicit peer-to-peer transfers and funnel account activity. Across the industry, compliance departments operate in a state of permanent defensive paranoia. According to a 2024 LexisNexis Risk Solutions study conducted by Forrester Consulting, financial crime compliance costs across the United States and Canada have reached USD 61 billion per year, with 99 percent of institutions reporting rising expenses and over 80 percent facing growing screening alert volumes.

To protect themselves from nine-figure regulatory fines, banks tune their automated monitoring rules to be hyper-sensitive. Those hair-trigger rules generate a mountain of false positives on ordinary people doing ordinary work, a friction point that even the FFIEC’s suspicious activity examination manual openly acknowledges. According to McKinsey’s research on financial crime operations, more than 90 percent of transaction-monitoring alerts at most banks turn out to be false positives, and banks report that as much as 85 percent of their anti-money laundering (AML) and financial crime activities remain manual, administrative, or nonanalytical, such as pulling data out of one internal system to key it into another. An empirical study of 19 major U.S. banks by the Bank Policy Institute illustrated the sheer scale of that funnel: participating institutions employed more than 14,000 compliance workers and reviewed roughly 16 million alerts in a single year to file 640,000 Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), with law enforcement following up on a median of just 4 percent of those filed reports. By Fiscal Year 2025, as documented in the FinCEN Year in Review, nationwide SAR filings climbed to roughly 4.8 million for the year, including 2.8 million reports filed by depository banks and another 1.26 million filed by money services businesses.

Here is the internal banking math that nobody explains to you at account opening. Every time an automated rule flags your incoming wire, a Level 1 compliance analyst has to open a ticket, pull your customer file, inspect your ledger, and decide whether to clear the alert or escalate it to a Level 2 investigator. Having a trained human read a foreign consulting contract, check a corporate registry in Estonia or Singapore, chase down customer documents, and write a formal audit memo justifying why a SAR was not filed consumes expensive specialist labor. Both the Wolfsberg Group’s statement on effective suspicious activity monitoring and FinCEN’s October 2025 interagency SAR FAQs have explicitly warned that over-alerting and defensive compliance routines drain real institutional resources on low-value noise.

When a low-fee checking account already sits near or below the bank’s USD 250 to USD 400 annual servicing break-even line, repeated manual compliance reviews and cross-border document checks quickly push that relationship deep into the red. Once a customer’s incremental compliance cost outweighs whatever modest deposit margin they bring in, banks do not hire extra analysts to study your freelance career. They simply "de-risk" you by restricting the account, mailing you a cashier’s check for your remaining balance, and terminating the relationship.

Regulators know this is happening, and they have called banks out on it repeatedly. In the United States, the Treasury Department’s 2023 strategy report on financial-sector de-risking confirmed that customer profitability, weighed directly against available compliance resources and AML system costs, is the primary driver behind institutions cutting off entire categories of customers. Across the Atlantic, the European Banking Authority’s guidelines on unwarranted de-risking and the global FATF policy statement on the risk-based approach both warn that wholesale offboarding of customer groups is a sign of ineffective risk management rather than sound compliance. Still, until regulators penalize banks as heavily for closing legitimate accounts as they do for missing money launderers, the unit economics inside your bank will not change.

Automated Transaction Monitoring Systems do not evaluate your character; they measure statistical deviation against predetermined rulesets. When independent professionals get locked out of their accounts, the review can almost always be traced back to one (or an ugly combination) of five mechanical triggers.

The most common self-inflicted wound I see among independent earners is what I call the Ghost Student Problem. Think back to when you actually opened your primary checking account. For many professionals in their late twenties or thirties, that account was opened eight or ten years ago when they were university students or entry-level local employees. During onboarding, you answered a quick questionnaire estimating your monthly deposit volume at USD 2,000 with zero international wire activity.

Fast-forward to today, and you are pushing USD 12,000 a month in cross-border software engineering or advisory retainers through that exact same account without ever updating your customer file. Under the FFIEC’s Customer Due Diligence examination rules, banks are required to build a customer risk profile at onboarding and use expected transaction types and volumes as the baseline for detecting suspicious activity. Those same examination standards identify unexplained changes in account activity and shifts in employment or business operations as direct triggers for event-driven risk reviews. The bank’s algorithm is not comparing your current income against the reality of your senior career. It is comparing a USD 12,000 international inflow against the stored baseline of a 20-year-old college student, flagging an immediate anomaly for activity inconsistent with the customer profile.

When you operate as a solo consultant or a one-person digital business, it is easy to view your revenue as your personal paycheck. To a bank’s risk engine, however, a salaried employee receiving domestic payroll and an independent contractor collecting client invoices belong in two completely different regulatory universes. Banks run separate monitoring models for retail consumers and commercial entities because business accounts naturally involve multiple counterparties, higher payment velocity, and international invoicing.

When you route Stripe payouts, platform settlements, or direct corporate wires into a standard personal checking account, you are feeding commercial transaction patterns into a consumer risk model. Worse, you are almost certainly violating the contract you signed when you opened the account. Traditional institutions like Associated Bank explicitly prohibit business activity in personal deposit agreements, and modern fintech platforms enforce the exact same boundary, as seen in Wise’s official rules separating personal and business accounts. Giving a bank a clear Terms of Service violation is the fastest way to get offboarded without appeal, because the institution does not even need to suspect illicit activity to close an account used in breach of its deposit contract.

Suppose a client pays you USD 5,000 on Tuesday morning into your primary bank or a multi-currency fintech app like Wise or Revolut. Because you manage your money actively, you log in two hours later and transfer USD 4,500 out to a brokerage account, a high-yield savings account at another institution, or a regulated crypto exchange. To a financially literate human, moving idle cash into higher-yielding assets immediately is smart personal treasury management.

To an anti-money laundering algorithm, near-zero balance retention paired with rapid inbound-to-outbound turnover closely mirrors the behavioral signature of a transit or funnel account. If you read the FFIEC’s official list of money-laundering red flags, one of the classic funds-transfer indicators is incoming deposits or transfers being received and "almost immediately, all or most of the transfers or deposits" being wired onward in a manner inconsistent with the customer’s history. Similarly, FinCEN’s advisory on funnel accounts highlights rapid withdrawals occurring with little time elapsing after deposits, while the FBI’s guidance on money mule networks explains how criminal syndicates use unwitting or complicit intermediaries to receive and forward funds to add layers of distance. Although FFIEC guidance notes that a single red flag is not proof of crime on its own, treating your checking account like a revolving door where money never rests overnight routinely trips pass-through velocity rules.

Modern remote work relies on a patchwork of global payment rails, and those rails often mangle the data your receiving bank needs to see. You might have one client paying you via SWIFT from London, another sending EUR via SEPA from Berlin, a third routing your retainer through a global payroll aggregator like Deel or Payoneer, and a fourth paying you in USDC or USDT stablecoins that you off-ramp into fiat through a licensed exchange.

Here is what happens under the hood when payments pass through intermediaries and payroll platforms. Instead of sending a direct wire from your client’s corporate bank account, many payment processors batch their payouts and disburse funds through local pooled accounts or net settlement rails. As detailed in the Wolfsberg Group’s 2026 guidance on banking non-bank payment service providers, bundled transactions and high levels of intermediation between the original payer and final beneficiary make it significantly harder for banks to screen counterparties and verify the underlying commercial flow. By the time an intermediated ACH or SEPA credit hits your bank, the original client’s name is often replaced in the header by a third-party payment processor or settlement bank, matching another FFIEC Appendix F red flag covering large third-party processor ACH credits from originators the receiving bank has never vetted. If you cash out stablecoin payroll from an exchange, the bank sees fiat arriving from a virtual asset platform, a flow that both FinCEN’s advisory on convertible virtual currencies and the FATF’s virtual asset red-flag report subject to heightened source-of-funds scrutiny whenever the bank lacks clear visibility into the underlying business activity.

Remote workers love the freedom to work from anywhere, but banking security engines are deeply territorial. When you log into your domestic banking app from a cafe Wi-Fi network in Bali, Lisbon, or Belgrade, or when you open your banking portal while connected to a commercial VPN node in another country, you trip a separate layer of defense: the fraud, e-banking, and sanctions screening engine.

As outlined in the FFIEC’s Electronic Banking examination overview, banks treat online banking outside their targeted geographic footprint as a heightened risk factor and actively monitor Internet Protocol (IP) address reports alongside funds-transfer velocity to spot account anomalies. Cybersecurity engines also track device fingerprints and network routing to stop account takeovers and enforce geographic sanctions. If your account logs in from Chicago on Monday morning and appears to log in from a shared VPN address in Southeast Asia or Eastern Europe four hours later, the system flags an "impossible travel" event or a high-risk jurisdiction login. Even when the lock starts as an automated fraud or sanctions precaution, unfreezing the account often triggers a manual back-office review of your recent ledger, turning a routine travel lock into a broader AML inquiry.

Nothing infuriates a legitimate freelancer more than the wall of silence that follows an account freeze. You call customer support in a panic because your rent is due, and the representative reads from a wooden script: "Your account is currently under review by a back-office team, and we cannot provide any further details or a timeline." When they eventually close the account, the termination letter usually cites a generic clause allowing either party to end the relationship at any time, giving you zero explanation of what triggered the decision.

Having trained bank staff on these exact protocols, I can tell you that the support agent on the phone is not trying to be cruel. First, frontline call center staff are intentionally locked out of the compliance case management system so they cannot accidentally leak investigative details. Second, and far more importantly, bank employees operate under the threat of severe criminal and civil penalties governed by strict anti-"tipping off" laws.

In the United States, the Bank Secrecy Act strictly forbids any bank director, officer, or employee from revealing to a customer that a Suspicious Activity Report has been filed or would reveal the existence of a SAR. As detailed in FinCEN’s official advisory on maintaining SAR confidentiality, unauthorized disclosure is a federal violation carrying civil penalties of up to USD 100,000 per violation and criminal penalties of up to USD 250,000 and five years in prison. In Europe, Article 39 of the EU Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive 2015/849) enforces the exact same prohibition against tipping off a customer that their transactions are being analyzed or reported to a Financial Intelligence Unit.

Historically, bank legal departments were so terrified of crossing tipping-off statutes that they instructed staff to say almost nothing during an inquiry. Regulators have recently tried to curb that overreaction; in a September 2026 joint statement on SAR confidentiality and customer communications, FinCEN and federal banking agencies clarified that banks are legally allowed to ask customers factual questions about specific transactions, engage transparently during fraud or account investigations, and communicate account closure decisions without revealing whether a SAR exists. Even so, many compliance departments still default to tight-lipped caution because saying nothing carries zero statutory disclosure risk for the bank.

No legitimate banking setup can guarantee zero compliance alerts, because banks recalibrate their monitoring models constantly and never publish their internal risk thresholds. What you can do is re-architect your financial structure so your cash flows match your declared customer profile, isolate higher-friction payment rails, and give compliance analysts the clean documentation they need to resolve a manual review without escalating toward account closure. Here is the five-step playbook I recommend to independent professionals and remote founders.

Never run your entire financial life through a single bank account. If your client wires, your tax reserves, your crypto off-ramps, and your grocery money all live inside one checking account, a single routine compliance hold can paralyze your ability to pay rent while the review plays out. Build operational firewalls across three distinct banking compartments at separate institutions:

Do not wait for an automated alert to discover that your bank still has you coded as a broke college student. Under the FFIEC’s ongoing Customer Due Diligence framework, banks evaluate higher-risk and cross-border relationships against specific profile attributes: occupation or type of business, source of funds, whether transactions are expected to be domestic or international, and expected transaction volumes. Fintech institutions follow the same logic upfront; Wise’s business verification rules, for example, explicitly collect your business activity details, expected monthly volumes, and counterparty countries, noting that fuller upfront information speeds up verification.

Whenever your career shifts toward self-employment, remote contracting, or higher foreign billings, log into your bank’s profile settings (or schedule a brief call with a relationship manager) before the first big wire arrives. Update your occupation to self-employed or independent consultant, describe your industry in plain terms (such as "B2B software engineering and cloud architecture consulting"), and update your expected monthly deposit range and counterparty regions. Having an updated KYC baseline will not bypass sanctions screening or shield unusual spikes from review, but it directly reduces avoidable alerts caused by outdated onboarding data.

Banks intentionally keep their exact transaction-monitoring lookback windows confidential so bad actors cannot structure transfers around them, whether a given ruleset evaluates 24-hour, 7-day, or 30-day rolling periods. That means there is no magic number of holding days guaranteed to prevent a velocity alert. Even so, treating a deposit account like an instant pass-through pipe is an unforced error.

When a client payment or platform payout lands in your account, resist the urge to sweep 90 percent of it out to an external brokerage, savings platform, or secondary bank within hours of arrival. Leaving a genuine operating reserve in your business account and consolidating outbound owner’s draws, tax set-asides, and brokerage transfers into one or two scheduled moves per month accomplishes two practical goals. First, it keeps your transaction pattern from mimicking the "almost immediately, all or most" onward transfer red flag highlighted in FFIEC Appendix F. Second, maintaining a healthy average balance gives the bank real deposit float to earn net interest income on, improving your standing inside the institution’s account-profitability math.

Payment messages are compliance documents, not chat threads. Under the Bank Secrecy Act’s recordkeeping and Travel Rule requirements detailed in the FFIEC Funds Transfers Recordkeeping manual, institutions handling funds transfers of USD 3,000 or more must retain and transmit specific originator, beneficiary, and payment instruction records. Globally, the Wolfsberg Group’s Payment Transparency Standards and its companion guidance on payment transparency roles and responsibilities emphasize that incomplete or "manifestly meaningless" payment message data impairs sanctions and AML screening and obligates institutions along the chain to monitor for missing details. Directly in FFIEC Appendix F, examiners flag wires that "contain limited content and lack related party information" or show "no apparent links to legitimate contracts, goods, or services."

Require every client to pay against a sequentially numbered PDF invoice showing both legal names, full addresses, a concrete description of the professional services rendered, the billing period, and the exact currency amount. Instruct clients to put a clear, specific reference in the wire remittance field (such as SWIFT MT103 Field 70 or the ISO 20022/SEPA remittance field), for example: "Invoice 2026-104 Cloud Architecture Consulting Oct 2026." A descriptive memo will not prevent an automated rule from firing on a new foreign corridor, and you cannot fix sender data that a third-party payroll processor strips upstream, which is why Step 5 matters. What clean payment references do prevent is avoidable ambiguity during initial alert triage, whereas blank memos, inside jokes, or mislabeling a commercial invoice as a "personal gift" invite immediate escalation.

When a bank or fintech platform sends you a Request for Information (RFI) or pauses a transfer for verification, response windows are often tight. As Wise’s customer verification guide and specialist business verification documentation standards explain, larger transfers, periodic regulatory refreshes, or specific business models routinely prompt specialist teams to pause a transfer or email requests for registration proof, recent bank statements, ownership records, or contracts demonstrating your source of funds. Trying to hunt down year-old agreements and reconcile processor fees while an incoming wire is frozen is a recipe for panic and inconsistent answers.

Create a dedicated, encrypted cloud folder right now and update a ready-to-deploy Compliance Dossier every quarter containing clean PDFs of four core items:

A well-organized PDF package will not override a bank’s risk appetite if an underlying client or jurisdiction violates internal policy. Where it makes a decisive difference is inside the manual workflow: remember McKinsey’s finding that up to 85 percent of bank AML work is bogged down in administrative data gathering. Handing a compliance analyst a single, indexed PDF package that reconciles every deposit to a signed contract and tax record eliminates weeks of back-and-forth document chasing and gives them a complete documentary trail to substantiate a lawful business purpose in their audit file. Doing this quarterly housekeeping also pays off when you apply for a mortgage, where underwriters audit self-employed bank statements with the exact same line-by-line skepticism.

The global economy has moved into the cloud, even if retail banking compliance still runs on 20th-century assumptions. You do not need to shrink your international ambitions or turn down foreign clients to stay banked. You just need to respect the unit economics inside the room, compartmentalize your cash flow, and keep a clean, verifiable paper trail ready whenever the risk engine comes knocking.

Written by Dora Milen, an economist and former commercial banker with 25 years of experience in traditional clearing systems.

#9953. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9952. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 10th of November 2026 04:55 PM

#9951. Running an Embedding Model Next to My Notes on an iPhone

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

I keep a lot of notes, and I rarely remember the words I used in them. In March I wrote a note called "Rent split with Arjun". In October I searched for "what does my flatmate owe". Keyword search found nothing, because the two share no words.

So when I built VB Notes, a markdown notes app where every note is a plain .md file in a folder you choose, search by meaning was the part I cared about most. I also wanted it to run on the device. Notes are private, and I wouldn't use a search box that sends every question to a server for my own notes.

This is what it took to run a 350-million-parameter embedding model next to the notes on an iPhone, and the same model on Mac, Windows and Linux.

The phone app is Expo and React Native, and the model runs through react-native-executorch. I wrote 18 questions, each worded differently from the note it should find, and ran them against the models the library ships:

The gap between the right note and an unrelated one mattered more to me than the hit rate. It decides how cleanly you can cut the list off. LFM2.5 became the default, MiniLM is the "Light" choice in Settings, and the multilingual model is there for people who write in more than one language.

LFM2.5 also reads a question and a note differently: questions go in with a query: prefix and notes with document: .

A model reads a limited number of words, so long notes are split into chunks: 200 words each for LFM2.5, each overlapping the previous one by a fifth, at most 16 per note. Every chunk starts with the note's title, so a paragraph deep inside "Trip to Ladakh" still knows it is about the trip.

Code blocks and Mermaid diagrams are left out. They are noise for meaning, and keyword search still finds them. Tags lose their # and count as words, so #work/clients still says what the note is about.

Each chunk becomes 1,024 numbers. As float32 that is 4 KB per chunk. I store each vector as int8 with one float32 scale in front: a quarter of the size, and the cosine similarity barely moves.

The vectors live in a SQLite file in the app's caches folder, out of iCloud backups. If iOS clears it, the app embeds the notes again. The .md files are always the source of truth.

At launch the app reads only each note's hash, to see what changed. The vectors load on the first search and stay in memory. The model itself waits three seconds after launch, unless you open Search first, so opening the app stays quick.

Cosine scores from a small model are not probabilities. A fixed floor of 0.3 sounded reasonable and dropped most of the right answers: short questions score between 0.15 and 0.3 even against the note they are about.

What works is two rules. Each model gets its own floor, at the level where unrelated notes stop (0.12 for LFM2.5). And a match is kept only if it is within 0.25 of the best match, up to ten matches.

Exact words still matter. If I type "Diamox", I want the note that says "Diamox" first. Keyword search is SQLite FTS5 on word starts, so "gro" finds "Groceries".

The two lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion: a note scores 1 / (60 + its rank) in each list, and the scores add up. A note found by both rises to the top, and a note found only by meaning still shows. I never have to compare a keyword score with a cosine score, which would be comparing two different things.

On the desktop, a single word only brings in meaning matches when no note contains it. One word gives the model little to go on, and the exact matches are what you want.

The first surprise was the download. I expected an iOS background download to be the right tool. On the simulator, the app's own download ran at 2.4 MB/s, while an iOS background session managed 0.05 to 0.9 MB/s.

So the download runs inside the app. The screen stays awake while it runs, and if you leave the app it stops, then carries on from the partial file when you come back.

The desktop app is Tauri 2 with Rust, not Electron. It uses the same model, as the official Q8_0 GGUF file (380 MB, checked by SHA-256 and downloaded on first launch), run by llama.cpp through the llama-cpp-2 crate: on Metal on Apple Silicon, on the CPU elsewhere, on its own thread.

Notes are chunked by the same TypeScript code as on the phone, and a background thread embeds them newest first, so recent notes become searchable first. The same chunks and the same model mean a question finds the same notes on both.

Try it: VB Notes is free and open source (MIT), for iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows and Linux. There is no account and no server: notes stay plain files, and search runs on your phone or computer.

I'd like to hear how you handle search in your own notes, and what would make you trust a model running next to them.

#9950. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.
