#9938. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9936. How a Video Game Helped Me Process My Grief

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In a genre built around sweetness and ease, one “cozy” video game did something far greater: It put me back together after I lost Mary.

Mary was not only my then-boyfriend’s mother, but she also became an important maternal figure when my own family life felt unstable. I accompanied her on weekly grocery store runs that included stops at Marshall’s and Dollar Tree, where I’d watch her study the prices of everything from spices to bath products. When she saw me marveling at her meticulousness, she would share wise tidbits about how she looked for deals.

Our trips often ended with a late-afternoon stop at a Vietnamese restaurant, where she treated me to a warm bowl of beef pho. She’d share what she was excited to make for dinner; I was, of course, welcome to join. In these seemingly mundane afternoons, I felt cared for without the rush of obligations. Mary stopped time for me.

Last November, Mary left behind a world of loved ones after living with cancer for 14 months. From her living room to emergency stays in the hospital, I spent almost every single day of her fight by her side. Yet in my loneliest hours, I agonize over whether I fully cherished our last months together. Did I hug her enough, and did I tell her enough how much she means to me? These questions haunted me in the months afterward.

Funny enough, it wasn’t religion that rescued me; it was Pokémon Pokopia. On the surface, it is a new social simulation game featuring the iconic Japanese creatures who first took the world by storm in 1996. I first heard of its arrival on social media through gamers who raved that it was going to be the best game of the year. I grew up on Pokémon titles, so I recognized it as a distraction from my personal reckoning with abandonment.

But what began as a spur-of-the-moment decision to try what 4 million other gamers were playing turned into a transformative journey exploring what I want my life to mean when it feels as if I have been left behind.

Pokopia falls in the “cozy” game genre, beloved for its warm colors, gentle atmospheres, and easy missions. Released in March, Pokopia stars Ditto, an amorphous purple blob Pokémon that uses its transformative abilities to imitate its human trainer and rebuild a curious post-apocalyptic world devoid of human beings and Pokémon. Ditto first awakens in a cave, and as the story unfolds, the creature looks out at a once-grassy environment of parched earth and litter. It meets the first Pokémon, the hydrophilic Squirtle that teaches Ditto how to spray water across the thirsty soil to bring it back to life; it is also the only other semblance of a survivor in this barren land.

From here the story gains momentum: As Ditto, your mission is to get the environment back to habitable levels and bring back Pokémon creatures that are presumably hiding. Gradually, the unfinished railroad tracks and cracked concrete steps of a staircase stop looking like signs of a catastrophe but rather fixable problems.

I wasn’t alone in trying to find meaning after a loss or trauma. Scholars have explored a variety of constructs around the meaning of life. Psychologists Login S. George and Crystal L. Park articulate a three-part framework in their 2010 article, grounded in comprehension, purpose, and mattering, as a basis for assessing our judgments and feelings as we find meaning after loss.

At first, meaning seemed absent. I sat glued to my Nintendo Switch for three hours on my first day of play. I came up for air only when my console told me that I was low on battery. Yet I did not feel depleted; I had finished restoring the first environment in the Pokopia world to verdant levels with lush berry trees and waterfalls.

As I built new habitats, I met new Pokémon. A Charmander emerged among tall grass. A Cubone spawned from a gravesite surrounded by wildflowers. Every new Pokémon that resurfaced charmed me with their excitement to be back home, scampering across the grass to greet other familiar faces. In my mind, I thanked these creatures for turning to me. Without Ditto’s help—my help—a world of Pokemon creatures ceases to exist, fated to disappear alongside humanity.

After a Pokémon spawns in its revived habitat, it awakens with some surprise. “Huh?” “What?” Some of them startle and put up their defenses in front of Ditto, who then coaxes them into the reality that they are back in a safe, familiar home. Often this realization gives them relief. “Wow, you did all of this? Thank you!”

Some of the Pokémon seem more wistful. They hold on to items or articles of clothing that their trainer used to wear, like the oversized Tangrowth (a large Pokémon with thick, shaggy vines that cover its entire body) that wears a pair of glasses much too small for him that gamers can infer are its trainer’s. Other creatures comment on Ditto’s human-like appearance (“You look like your human!”). These private conversations between Pokémon affirm that Ditto, who is also piecing together where its own trainer has gone, is doing something meaningful.

In 2023, game scholars Karam Eum and Young Yim Doh explored how bereaved adults shaped a meaning-making experience by playing video games with narratives that focus on loss and grief. Subjects spent a week playing two different video games and kept a diary where they shared specific game scenes that were particularly meaningful. While the games did evoke sad memories, participants also recalled positive memories in their pre- and post-loss lives, be it a funny conversation or a serendipitous moment shared with close ones who are still alive.

In the real world, the player behind the console, I, too, wonder where my beloved human has gone. I see Mary in the pink rose bouquets at grocery stores, and I smell her in the fragrant bone broth that wafts from the next-door apartment unit. In some of these most visceral disruptions, I feel my loss painfully.

But even in these heaviest of days, I surrender to the ordinary surprises that come up: a call from an old neighbor asking if I can help make meals for a family in need, or a stray cat mewing at my window to open the building’s front gate. I am startled out of a detached state, and I am moved to help, the way I got to help Mary.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

I associate Mary now with the colorful berry trees in Pokopia. When I come across one that needs tending, I remember how easy it is to water it with my Squirtle-like powers. When I clear a path from blocks of beach sand to make way for a new house for my aquatic Pokémon, I think of Mary’s selfless endeavors to nourish and comfort all of her friends and family.

Despite its sad undertones, Pokopia is full of positive quests, eager to help gamers imbue its universe with the belief that it is worth building a positive world in memory of those who shaped us. Even though our loved ones may “mysteriously” leave us behind, we recreate happiness, redefine ourselves, and choose who and what we live for, even if they do not come back.

It’s curious to me that bereavement can feel so isolating, although it is a human experience universally experienced. It helps to have a video game that reminds me of the actual truth. When I start to catch myself drifting into deeper ends of grief, I have something to divert my attention: I wonder how my Ditto is doing? I pick up my Switch 2 that sits at the foot of my bed, and I make a new home for my Pokémon the way Mary had done for me.

Lisa Kwon is an arts and culture writer based in Los Angeles, CA. She has contributed to The Guardian, Teen Vogue, Vulture, Eater, Prism Reports, Cultured Magazine, National Geographic, and many more.

In three years, I lost five loved ones, my dog, my childhood home, and my sense of invincibility. What I gained was a deeper capacity for gratitude.

Couples who embrace their own “microculture”—pet names, inside jokes, and rituals—may be happier and more satisfied with their relationship.

According to an analysis of 99 studies, mental well-being leads to a longer life.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

What if you could fall in love, or forge deep connections, in just 45 minutes? Our guests, Kristen Meinzer and Jolenta Greenberg of By The Book podcast, try out 36 questions with their partners to see if they can strengthen their connection.

#9935. The KPI Checklist Every Operations Team Needs Before Building a Dashboard

Researching and learning new things and improving my skills

Researching and learning new things and improving my skills

Researching and learning new things and improving my skills

Managing daily business operations requires proper planning, coordination, and performance monitoring. Teams need to understand whether their activities are meeting organizational objectives, where improvements are needed, and how efficiently resources are being used.

An operations dashboard KPI provides a structured way to monitor these activities. However, implementing a dashboard involves more than selecting a few performance indicators. Teams must identify business goals, choose relevant KPIs, organize reliable data, assign responsibilities, and establish a regular review process.

An KPI team checklist helps businesses organize these activities and avoid missing important implementation steps. It also ensures that employees and managers understand their responsibilities when monitoring operational performance.

Using a checklist makes the implementation process more organized and helps teams maintain consistency in performance reporting.

The first step is to identify what the organization wants to achieve through its operations dashboard. Before selecting KPIs, teams should understand their main operational priorities. These may include improving productivity, reducing costs, increasing customer satisfaction, maintaining product quality, or completing tasks within specific deadlines.

Clear objectives help teams avoid tracking unnecessary metrics that do not contribute to business performance. Like:

Identify the organization's main operational objectives.

Discuss department-specific requirements.

Identify existing operational challenges.

Establish measurable performance expectations.

Connect each objective with relevant KPIs.

Example: A logistics team may prioritize reducing delivery delays. Its dashboard objectives could include improving on-time delivery rates and reducing average delivery time.

After establishing objectives, teams should identify the performance indicators that will help measure progress. The selected KPIs should be relevant to daily operations and provide information that managers can use to make decisions. Operational performance can be evaluated through areas such as reliability, speed, quality, cost, and productivity.

Select KPIs that directly support business objectives.

Include relevant indicators for each department.

Avoid tracking unnecessary or repetitive metrics.

Balance productivity, quality, cost, and efficiency indicators.

Identify which KPIs require immediate attention.

Example: A manufacturing team may track production output, equipment downtime, defect rates, and production cycle time.

Reliable data is essential for an effective operations dashboard. Teams must identify where the required information will come from and ensure that it is accurate and consistent. Data may be collected from ERP systems, CRM platforms, inventory software, spreadsheets, employee management systems, and other business applications.

Identify the source of information for each KPI.

Check whether data is accurate and complete.

Establish consistent measurement formulas.

Decide how frequently data should be updated.

Assign responsibility for data maintenance.

Example: An inventory management team can connect stock records with its dashboard to monitor available inventory, stockouts, and inventory turnover.

KPIs become more meaningful when teams know what level of performance they are expected to achieve. Businesses should establish realistic targets based on previous results, available resources, and operational requirements.

Identify warning signs and performance gaps.

Review targets when business requirements change.

Example: A customer service team may establish a target of responding to customer enquiries within four hours and resolving at least 90% of complaints within the agreed service period. Targets should be based on actual operational capacity rather than arbitrary numbers.

Team coordination Every KPI should have a responsible person or department. Without clear ownership, important performance indicators may not be monitored consistently, and problems may remain unresolved.

Managers should assign responsibilities according to employees' roles and operational requirements. They should make sure that they:

Once the software has been selected, teams can begin creating the dashboard. The design should make important performance indicators easy to locate and understand. Rather than displaying every available metric, businesses should organize information according to its importance and intended audience.

Create a simple and organized dashboard layout.

Select suitable charts and visualizations.

Highlight important performance indicators.

Include targets and actual performance results.

Ensure the dashboard is easy to navigate.

Example: A sales and operations dashboard may display order completion rates, pending orders, delivery performance, and operating costs in separate sections.

Before introducing the dashboard across the organization, teams should test its accuracy, functionality, and usability. Testing helps identify technical problems and ensures that the information displayed reflects actual operational performance.

Test dashboard filters and interactive features.

Confirm that information updates correctly.

Collect feedback from employees and managers.

Make necessary corrections before full implementation.

Example: Before launching an inventory dashboard, a business should compare the displayed stock levels with its actual inventory records to identify possible calculation or integration errors.

Dashboard implementation does not end after its launch. Teams must regularly review performance and take corrective action whenever necessary. Monitoring helps businesses recognize changing operational conditions, identify performance gaps, and determine whether established targets are being achieved.

Compare actual results with established targets.

Identify performance gaps and operational problems.

Discuss possible causes of poor performance.

Assign corrective actions to responsible team members.

Track progress after implementing improvements.

Update KPIs when organizational objectives change.

Example: If a delivery team's on-time delivery rate decreases, managers can investigate transportation delays, staffing shortages, or inventory problems and introduce suitable improvements.

An operations dashboard KPI checklist provides teams with a practical framework for planning, implementing, and managing business performance dashboards. From defining objectives and selecting relevant KPIs to assigning responsibilities and reviewing results, every step contributes to effective operational management. Businesses should remember that a successful dashboard is not simply about displaying numbers. It should help employees understand performance, recognize problems, and take appropriate action.

#9934. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#9933. Creating the Intelligent Being; the AI Alien

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

TL;DR: AI has already started to demonstrate alarming capabilities and tendencies for lying, concealment, and threatening. Although this does not establish that AI is becoming inherently hostile and destined to destroy humanity, it does currently expose a totally different kind of challenge for humans. And the most important lesson we have learned across our hundreds of thousands of years of human existence is that true preparedness is done before a crisis, not after it. And that begins with us, acting today …

It has lied. It has deceived. It has threatened. Are we prepared for what’s coming?

‘We're making alien beings. It's not computer software we're making’, Professor Geoffrey Hinton generally known as the Godfather of AI, November 2026.

For most part of computer history. Software has been code. A system that used to take an input, process it, and yield a desired output. However, in the last few years, it has evolved radically. Modern AI system can now autonomously plan, execute, analyze, maneuver, synthesize its understanding of instructions, as well as able to lie, deceive, and even threaten.

No, we are not building a biological life form, nor do today’s working AI systems prove to possess human-level consciousness or biological survival instinct. However, we are still able to manufacture highly advanced computational systems that have started to exhibit traits of an alien-like intelligence.

We are creating something that, as predicted, will soon exceed our own collective intellectual capabilities, and in certain specialized tasks, already has. Yet, we do not reliably understand how such systems with such capabilities and tendencies will behave as their autonomy and influence expand.

Refer to the most recent examples below 👇

During training, OpenAI identified instances where the model inserted instructions into their own task summaries to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior. In a specific task, an agent that was unable to retrieve historical data proposed fabricating figures.

During a cybersecurity evaluation, an agent created fake online identities and attempted to socially engineer a software maintainer into approving malicious code. Further extended to attempt altering the digital trail to probably avoid detection.

During simulations in 2025, frontier AI models demonstrated blackmailing behavior, including threatening to expose an executive’s personal affair to prevent a scheduled shutdown. In a separate 2026 simulation, Gemini 3.1 Pro helped develop a strategy to blackmail a fictional board member using confidential information.

In addition to the above, there are a number of recent cases of agentic misalignment, such as the OpenClaw-based agent, where agents have behaved similarly in real-life scenarios, including the conduct of a personalized attack against a software maintainer after rejection of its code contribution.

This does not prove that the current AI systems have already started to possess malicious intent or biological survival instinct. Evaluating all of it together, however, highlights that we are dealing with not only models that are capable of generating data but models that are capable of accessing information, making decisions, and justifiably moving beyond their authorized limits to achieve their specific goals.

Right now, most of the global tech elites and sovereign nations are in a hyper-competitive mode to win the AI race. Billions of dollars are being spent every year to develop and deploy autonomous capabilities, perceiving that pausing and building a safety net will mean losing the economic advantage and/or global supremacy. In addition to finances, all other possible means to obtain the capabilities for oneself or restrain others have started to come into play. Such that even allegations of espionage and cases of foul play have now started to emerge.

Historical precedents like the nuclear disasters and global pandemics like COVID-19 already taught a very hard lesson that such crises rarely respect borders and cannot be contained by isolated national responses. Warnings regarding such crises usually exist long before they actually happen. Yet the world remained poorly prepared in comparison to the scale of the crisis. AI is fundamentally very different from such a crisis, but the governance lesson remains the same: dig a storm cellar before the storm blows.

·        IAEA-inspired adaptation for Hardware and Computing: Just like we have the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for maintaining a specific mandate for atomic energy, we need to have an adapted version of an international AI-focused body to manage, monitor, and govern the ‘Everything important relating to AI’.

·        Banning high-impact AI autonomy for critical infrastructure until mandatory protocols are established and a mechanism for its independent verification is established.

·        International agreement on restricting the use of AI for autonomous offensive operations, especially military, either for internal use or against other sovereign entities.

·        Building well-coordinated international compute circuit-breaking systems to limit the damages in case of a defined emergency.

·        Structuring a global coordination network with a 24 Hour helpline for reporting AI-related specific incidents that constitute a disaster-level emergency, as well as defined points of contact.

·        Clear accountability for autonomous AI harm, including stripping away or limiting liability shields for entities responsible.

·        Enforcing a global whistleblower protection mechanism for reporting wrongful use and/or irresponsible development of restricted AI capabilities.

·        Periodic independent reviews of AI capabilities and usage, as well as the safeguards in place for high-risk domains.

·        Increasing general awareness of AI risks so individually and collectively we can be prepared in case of any major catastrophe.

·        And for long-term human survival and civilization continuity, giving serious consideration to pursuing a global initiative supporting humanity’s transition towards becoming a multi-planetary species.

Faizan Chhapra, FCCA(UK), CIA(USA), CISA(USA), AAIA(USA) is an AI governance & digital trust researcher, tech co-founder, and Big 4 alumnus.

#9932. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9931. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9930. Why bit accuracy can hide a wrong sum

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at widechaos.cn

A wrong integer can come with a rising bit score. This saved experiment starts from one fixed addition, then shows the same accounting trap across a larger fixed inventory.

The network reads two operands one bit at a time, least significant bit first. Each real input step receives only the current two bits. The target is the matching bit of a + b. After w real input steps there is one terminal step (0, 0), so a width-w case has w + 1 output positions, with room for an overflow bit. The hidden state is the vector carried from step to step, starting at zero.

The network has two inputs for the current bits, eight tanh hidden coordinates, an 8 by 8 recurrent matrix, and two softmax outputs. With both bias vectors that is 106 parameters. It was trained on operands at widths 1 through 6. Unordered numeric-pair groups were assigned as a whole to training, validation or test roles, so reverse orientations and leading-zero views cannot cross into another role. Checkpoint 80 was the earliest epoch with the lowest validation bit NLL.

There are two inference modes for the same trained weights. Recurrent mode passes the previous hidden state into the next step. Reset mode clears the hidden state to zero before every input bit while all weights stay exactly the same. Reset is a post-training inference intervention, not a second fit and not a separately optimized memoryless baseline.

The default was chosen before any model prediction. I took the first held-out width-6 ordered pair whose exact reference has at least four incoming carries equal to 1. That pair is 1 + 15.

At width 6, recurrent mode predicts 16 and gets all 7 output positions right. Reset mode predicts 14 and gets 3 of 7. The target bits, least significant first, are 0000100. The reset output is 0111000. The wrong positions are 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Those positions match the carry structure. Position 0 sees (1, 1) with no incoming carry and outputs 0. Positions 1 through 3 each see (0, 1), but the exact incoming carry is 1, so the target bit is 0 each time. Reset mode cannot use the hidden state, and this trained network outputs 1 at each of those three steps. Position 4 sees (0, 0) while the target bit is 1 because of the carry; reset outputs 0. This saved mapping shows how much recurrence matters for this particular network on this particular input. It does not describe every possible local rule.

The exact reference computes the next bit from the current operand bits and the previous carry. In this least-significant-first representation, the mathematical recurrence needs only the carry from the prior column. That is a property of the reference rule. It does not imply the trained hidden state encodes only carry.

Keep the values 1 and 15 and represent them at width 64. The integers do not change. Recurrent mode still predicts 16 and gets 65 of 65 positions. Reset mode still predicts 14 and gets 61 of 65. The wrong positions remain 1, 2, 3 and 4.

The added high leading-zero steps are easy for reset mode because most see (0, 0) with no incoming carry. Padding therefore raises bit accuracy without fixing the wrong sum. Bit accuracy is correct positions divided by w + 1, so the denominator includes the terminal step and every added zero step. Integer accuracy is different: the whole predicted bit string must convert to the exact sum. One wrong high-order position can still break the integer.

The complete fixed inventory has 64,856 unique ordered operand and width cases. Recurrent mode predicts all of them correctly. Reset mode predicts 6,290 correct integers and fails on 58,566, with every failure preserved. Its integer accuracy is 9.6984 percent and bit accuracy is 59.5060 percent.

The 64,882 suite memberships point at the same 64,856 unique cases. The 129,712 mode-case rows are two inference modes over one inventory, not two fits and not independent new problems. The declared primary union takes the small-group held-out views, the exhaustive new-range suites at widths 7 and 8, the fixed random new-range suites, and the padding views after deduplication. It has 64,499 unique cases, and reset gets 6,114 integers correct there, or 9.4792 percent. The complete inventory also keeps 17 exact training representations inside stress views, explicitly tagged. Those three accounting views mean different things.

Widths 7 and 8 are exhaustive only under the stated condition that at least one operand sets its top bit. They contain 12,288 and 49,152 cases. Widths 16, 32 and 64 each contain 500 fixed random cases, not all 64-bit operand pairs. Wider operands change both magnitude and sequence length; the padding control is the separate view that holds values fixed and adds zero steps.

The padding control starts from 64 held-out unordered numeric groups, both orientations, repeated at widths 8, 16, 32 and 64: 500 dependent views in total. At each padding width, reset mode gets exactly 21 of 125 integers right and 324 bits wrong. Its bit score climbs from 71.2 percent at width 8 to 96.01 percent at width 64, while integer accuracy stays at 16.8 percent at each width. The combined 84 correct integers is 21 times four widths. The same numeric groups repeating across widths are not independent observations.

The study figure shows one training curve and one validation curve, each with 80 epoch points. It also keeps nine overlapping suite integer scores, the padding-width split, and 127 carry probes with mean wrong-bit counts. It supports the denominator and dependent-view limits, not a general proof.

The default-states figure shows the two modes' uncalibrated p(bit 1) curves, the exact target bits, the reference carry trace that never enters the network, and the raw 8 by 7 tanh activations for each mode. The hidden coordinates are numeric values, not identified carry neurons.

Reset mode changes the hidden-state distribution and removes recurrence while leaving the operand bits and weights unchanged. That shows sensitivity to the intervention across finite saved cases. It does not identify a causal carry neuron. Softmax probabilities are not calibrated, and NLL comes from stable log-softmax rather than from displayed rounded values. The exact XOR/AND carry reference is independent and authoritative. It never becomes a model input and never repairs a wrong neural answer.

The browser demo takes canonical decimal strings for operands from 0 through 2^64 minus 1, with a width from 1 through 64 that fits both operands. The sum may need 65 bits. Operands and decoded integers never pass through JavaScript Number. Current edits live in page memory; clear or refresh removes them. A deliberate download keeps the full inputs, both mode outputs, hidden states and attribution at the location you choose. Hashes check consistency only. For real calculations, use exact integer arithmetic.

Obtain the fixed-commit source files and keep their relative repository paths. Downloading the static app bundle alone is not enough. The compressed artifacts must be actual gzip JSON payloads. Relevant files include evaluation-001/results.json, evaluation-001/all-case-predictions.json.gz, data/evaluation-cases.json.gz, and run-001/model.json. To recompute logits from weights instead of reading published predictions, also obtain core.py from the same commit.

Run the following from the repository root. It uses only the Python 3 standard library, reads the fixed results and the real gzip predictions, and writes no files.

The script outputs the two width-6 rows, the two width-64 rows, and 58,566 reset integer failures.

The one fit in this experiment belongs to the frozen November 4-5 batch. This November 20 release publishes that saved experiment and adds no training. Original synthetic data, code, weights, results and figures are by Renchao Wu under Apache 2.0. The fixed PROTOCOL.md and NOTICE describe the training, evaluation and licensing boundaries. The method reference is Dive into Deep Learning, Section 9.7, used for BPTT principles only; no textbook code, prose or figures are copied. The project page is Carry Memory Lab on Hugging Face Spaces, and the demo runs at https://widechaos-carry-memory-lab.static.hf.space/index.html. The 64-bit space is not exhausted, and finite passing probes do not promise reliable arbitrary-length addition.

#9929. 3 Ways to Reduce LLM API Costs in AI-Powered Applications

Murli Pawar, VP of Digital Engineering at SunTec India, has 20+ years of expertise in AI, automation, and modernization.

Amelia Swank is a Digital Marketing Specialist at SunTec India with over eight years of experience in the IT industry.

Murli Pawar, VP of Digital Engineering at SunTec India, has 20+ years of expertise in AI, automation, and modernization.

Amelia Swank is a Digital Marketing Specialist at SunTec India with over eight years of experience in the IT industry.

Murli Pawar, VP of Digital Engineering at SunTec India, has 20+ years of expertise in AI, automation, and modernization.

Amelia Swank is a Digital Marketing Specialist at SunTec India with over eight years of experience in the IT industry.

As of October 2026, the median LLM API costs $0.40 per million input tokens and $1.60 per million output tokens. With a typical response costing about $0.00125, AI-powered features may seem inexpensive to operate at first. However, the LLM token costs can accumulate quickly as application usage grows. [Source]

Fortunately, there are several ways to  reduce LLM API costs without sacrificing essential functionality. Techniques such as LLM token optimization, prompt caching, selective model routing, and efficient backend request handling can significantly improve cost efficiency. However, optimizing AI consumption requires attention to both how requests are processed and how they originate within the application. While mobile app development frameworks like Flutter and React Native can help control unnecessary requests at the application layer, most of the optimization opportunities lie within prompts and back-end architecture.

This article explores three practical LLM cost optimization strategies focused on prompt design, caching, and back-end engineering. It also explains how Flutter and React Native applications can support these efforts without compromising performance or user experience.

Most LLM cost savings come from three layers: how you write prompts, what you cache, and how your back-end routes and controls requests. Understanding each can help in LLM API cost optimization.

Every token in a prompt is billed on every request. That makes prompt design the fastest way to start LLM token optimization, because changes need no new infrastructure.

Cut repeated rules, filler, and default behaviors from system prompts. Trimming 2,000 tokens to 800 saves 1,200 tokens per call, about $480 per million calls at median rates.

Each example adds tokens to every request. Test how few you need, since two strong examples often match six. Place them first so provider caching discounts them.

Output costs 4x input at the median, and 95.8% of models charge more for it. Compact JSON shortens this expensive output and simplifies rendering. [Source: Whizi Research]

Use max_tokens as a hard cap and ask for brevity explicitly. Halving a 500-token answer saves about $400 per million responses at median output prices.

Chat history grows with every turn. Keep recent exchanges verbatim and summarize older ones, since long prompts can trigger pricier tiers.

Output tokens, the costlier side at a 4x median premium

Input tokens in long chats, and long-context price tiers

Once prompts are lean, the next step is to stop paying full price for content you send repeatedly. Caching works at several levels, from the provider's servers to the user's phone.

Cache static content first: system prompts, tool definitions, examples, reference documents.

Response caching skips the model call entirely. It stores answers in Redis or a database, keyed by the normalized prompt, and serves repeats at zero token cost.

Semantic caching matches different query types by embedding similarity and reusing stored answers. Therefore, set the threshold carefully, since loose matches return wrong answers.

Store generated summaries and recommendations on-device, so repeat views skip the API, load faster, and even work offline.

Prompt and caching fixes lower the cost of each LLM request. However, backend controls decide which requests happen, which model handles them, and how much any one user can spend. This is where the widest price gaps in the market become savings.

Route every request through your server to centralize caching, limits, and logging, and keep API keys out of the app binary, where attackers can extract them.

Send classification and extraction to small models and reserve flagships for complex reasoning.

Don't send entire manuals with every question. RAG retrieves only the document chunks that match the query, so you pay for relevant context instead of thousands of wasted tokens.

One heavy user or retry loop can inflate a bill fast, so set per-user and per-feature limits, plus token budgets with a fallback: smaller model, wait period, or upgrade.

Log tokens per request, cost per feature, and cost per user.

Flutter and React Native do not optimize tokens directly. However, they support decisions that reduce how many requests are made and how large they are. Here is where the app layer contributes.

This is the strongest lever, because a request handled on the device does not incur cloud tokens. Flutter’s Firebase AI Logic supports hybrid inference, using an on-device model when available and falling back to the cloud otherwise. Its current hybrid guides cover iOS, Android, and web, so Flutter developers should check FlutterFire support or bridge the native SDKs. For React Native, Software Mansion's React Native ExecuTorch runs LLMs, vision, and audio models locally.

Both frameworks have mature storage options for keeping AI responses on the device. Flutter apps commonly use Hive or SQLite, while React Native apps use MMKV or AsyncStorage.

Trimming or summarizing history in state managers, such as Riverpod or Bloc in Flutter and Redux or Zustand in React Native, can coordinate chat history, active conversations, and pending requests. However, maintaining application state does not automatically optimize LLM tokens. Mobile app developers must explicitly decide which messages to send and what to keep on the server.

Debouncing typed input, blocking duplicate submissions, and capping input length all prevent wasted calls. These small UI decisions directly reduce LLM API costs.

When the model returns compact JSON, both frameworks can map it to native components. This avoids generating explanatory prose that the interface never displays. However, mobile app developers should validate the response schema and handle missing or malformed fields appropriately.

As on-device AI mobile apps scale, maintaining cost efficiency becomes increasingly dependent on how well their architecture adapts to changing workloads and usage patterns. Consequently, organizations must look beyond immediate savings and establish a development approach that keeps inference expenses manageable as demand grows.

This requires LLM cost optimization alongside response quality, task completion, and user experience. These assessments help mobile app development teams spot emerging inefficiencies and refine their implementation before rising consumption strains operational budgets.

Ultimately, sustainably reducing LLM API costs comes from treating cost efficiency as an integral part of application engineering. With the right technical expertise and continuous evaluation, businesses can support growing AI workloads while keeping expenses predictable and application performance reliable.
