#9928. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

  • You get paid the same day you make a sale. Sellfy doesn't delay your funds as some other payment processors do.

  • The file security features can help you protect your digital property by allowing you to put PDF stamps, set download limits, and SSL encryption.

#9927. What Bystanders Can Do to Stop Sexual Violence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

As an undergrad student decades ago, I attended a dorm presentation describing the importance of giving and receiving sexual consent. The workshop leaders explained that if your partner said “no” or “stop” but you proceeded to have sex anyway, it was considered rape.

A high-profile athlete on campus raised his hand and said, in utter disbelief, “That can’t be right. By that definition, everyone I’ve ever had sex with I’ve raped.”

I was horrified by his comment, but most students laughed. He clearly saw nothing wrong with the view he’d expressed, presumably believing it was widely shared.

I immediately thought of this experience when I heard about the alleged sexual assault committed by seven fraternity members at Cornell University. As a social psychologist, and the author of a book examining why so-called good people stay silent in the face of problematic behavior, what I find most tragic about the events at Cornell is that reportedly over 50 men on a group chat learned about the assault as it was happening. Yet there’s been no public report that any of them tried to stop the assault, help the victim, or contact campus or local police departments.

This type of inaction is very common. In about one-third of sexual assaults, at least one other person is present who potentially could intervene but in most instances chooses not to. Why?

Data suggests a minority of men actually commit sexual assault. Researchers estimate about 6.5% of male college students in the United States and Canada have committed rape. Yet many men who find sexual violence offensive mistakenly believe that other men do not.

Undergraduate men in one study reported their beliefs about common rape myths, such as “If a girl doesn’t physically fight back, you can’t really say it was rape,” and “If a girl goes to a room alone with a guy at a party, it is her own fault if she is raped.” Researchers then asked participants how they thought both their close friends and average male college students would answer these same questions.

The results provided clear evidence that college men have skewed views of what those around them are thinking. Most students saw their classmates and friends as more supportive of rape myths than they themselves were.

Unfortunately, believing that other men generally accept sexual violence—even when this belief is wrong—inhibits their willingness to intervene to stop such behavior when they encounter it. In fact, men’s beliefs about their peers’ attitudes are a stronger predictor of their willingness to intervene than their own stated attitudes about sexual aggression.

Men who underestimate their peers’ discomfort with sexually aggressive behavior often fear the consequences of calling out problematic views or intervening in the face of inappropriate behavior. The most common reason male college students give for failing to intervene in situations involving sexual violence is a fear of being laughed at or ridiculed—in particular, a desire not to appear weak to other men.

Men who actually commit assault also tend to overestimate support for such behavior. Not surprisingly, men who report having committed sexual assault believe that other men are more accepting of such behavior and have engaged in such behavior themselves.

This assumed support leads them to feel comfortable describing problematic behavior, which leads other men to believe that sexual violence is more common, and more accepted, than it actually is.

Given the consistent evidence that men wrongly believe that most men are more comfortable with sexual violence than they themselves are, the challenge is not to change the social norm. It’s getting people to see what it actually already is.

Correcting such misperceptions can go a long way toward reducing sexual violence. First-year male college students who participate in a 90-minute sexual assault prevention program—focused on refuting rape myths, increasing awareness of the importance of consent, and correcting misperceptions about other men’s attitudes and behaviors—report reduced levels of sexual aggression themselves four months later.

These programs work in two ways. First, men who receive accurate information about what other men actually believe are less inhibited about speaking out and intervening. Second, men who are at risk of engaging in sexual aggression may change their intentions after learning that their peers do not support such behavior.

At the same time, men in tight-knit groups feel considerable pressure to show loyalty to other group members, which may lead to ignoring bad behavior committed by their peers.

But the underlying dynamics of peer influence can help shift group norms from protecting group members by staying silent to stepping in to prevent bad behavior. One college football player described looking out for his teammates, even if that meant interrupting a potential sexual encounter: “Maybe you don’t get the girl, but you’ll keep your scholarship and still be on the team.”

Another approach for preventing sexual assault is to learn strategies for intervening. Bystander intervention programs emphasize the importance of stopping bad behavior before it escalates, teach specific skills for intervening, and remind people that everyone has a responsibility to prevent sexual violence.

Students who participate in such programs are more confident in their ability to intervene and more willing to do so. Most importantly, rates of sexual violence are markedly lower on campuses that have implemented these programs. For example, one study found that experiences of sexual harassment and stalking were 11% lower and that instances of unwanted sexual activity with women who were too drunk or high to stop them were as much as 17% lower.

It’s tempting to read about the Cornell case and assume the apparent inaction in the face of problematic behavior is uniquely a problem at one college, or only with members of fraternities, or only with college students. But the reality is that pretty much everyone has been in situations where they’ve seen potentially problematic behavior and failed to speak up.

Understanding the very normal psychological factors that lead people to misperceive what others are actually thinking and feeling—and learning specific strategies for intervening—can make a real difference.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

is the Poler Family Professor of Psychology at Amherst College. Her latest trade book, published in North America as Why We Act: Turning Bystanders Into Moral Rebels (Harvard University Press) and internationally as The Bystander Effect: The Psychology of Courage and Inaction (HarperCollins), examines why good people so often stay silent or do nothing in the face of wrongdoing.

#9926. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

#9925. SUMIF vs SUMIFS: when to use each (with real examples)

SUMIF and SUMIFS look almost identical, and that's exactly why people mix them up. The difference is small but trips up almost everyone once: the position of the sum range changes.

Here's the clean rule, with examples you can paste straight into Excel.

That's it. One condition → SUMIF. Two or more → SUMIFS. But because the sum range moves, copying a SUMIF into a SUMIFS without rearranging arguments silently sums the wrong column.

If you omit the sum range, SUMIF sums the criteria range itself — handy for "sum all values greater than 100":

Sum sales where region is "East" and product is "Widget":

Notice the sum range B2:B100 jumped to the front. Each condition is a pair: criteria_range, then criteria. All conditions must be true (AND logic).

This treats A2:A100 as the sum range and "East" as a criteria_range — it errors or sums nonsense. The fix is mechanical: move the column you want to total to the first argument.

That last row matters: SUMIFS is AND-only. For OR, add two SUMIFS together (or use SUMPRODUCT).

Reading the argument order once isn't enough — you have to type it a few times before it sticks. I built a free browser lab where you edit the formula and see the result update instantly, no signup:

And if you want a printable set of exercises (with answer key) covering lookups, text, dates and statistics, there's a free workbook here: LookupLab practice exercises.

One condition → SUMIF, sum range last. Two-plus → SUMIFS, sum range first. When a sum "looks wrong," check the argument order before you check the data — it's almost always the sum range in the wrong slot.

#9924. DeepSeek's GRPO in 2026: What's Changed Since the Original Paper

DeepSeek's published 2026 V4 report still uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train domain specialists, but it changes the wider post-training pipeline. Specialists are first adapted with supervised fine-tuning and domain-specific GRPO; a later on-policy distillation stage transfers their capabilities into a unified model. The important change is therefore architectural: GRPO remains part of specialist training, while distillation replaces the previous mixed-RL stage for the final unified model.

The calendar's exact backlink is DeepSeek's GRPO approach. Eigenform works on recursive self-improvement in AI and LLM agents, a related research area where reinforcement-learning objectives, agent behaviour and evaluation quality all influence how systems improve. Its research and applied-AI work also highlights the importance of testing changes against evidence from the environment.

Eigenform focuses on recursive self-improvement in AI agents and related training research. GRPO is not an Eigenform method; it is a DeepSeek-associated reinforcement-learning algorithm. The connection is the engineering problem of using feedback while keeping updates measurable and stable.

GRPO compares a group of candidate responses to the same prompt. Each response receives a reward, and its advantage is calculated relative to the other responses in that group. The policy is updated using a clipped objective and reference-policy regularisation. Unlike PPO, GRPO does not require a separate value critic; group statistics provide the baseline.

That group-relative idea remains central. It is important not to describe every change in a model's training pipeline as a change to the GRPO algorithm itself. In practical terms, the published V4 recipe can be summarised as three steps:

V3.2: mixed reinforcement learning DeepSeek-V3.2 used GRPO in a mixed RL stage covering reasoning, agent and human-alignment tasks, with rule-based rewards and generative reward models. V4: specialist training followed by distillation The DeepSeek-V4 technical report describes specialist training followed by on-policy distillation. Domain specialists are adapted with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO using domain-specific prompts and reward signals. The final unified model is then distilled from those specialists. The report says this replaces the mixed reinforcement-learning stage used in the earlier pipeline; it does not say GRPO itself has disappeared from specialist training.

The group-relative principle remains for specialist RL, while final consolidation uses on-policy distillation. V4 places GRPO inside a more modular recipe rather than replacing it with a new GRPO algorithm. “The mixed Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage was entirely replaced by On-Policy Distillation.” — DeepSeek-V4 technical report

DeepSeek's V4 report still uses GRPO to train domain-specific experts after SFT, then uses on-policy distillation to combine those experts into a unified model. The core group-relative optimisation idea remains; the system-level post-training pipeline has evolved.

GRPO remains in DeepSeek's specialist-training stage, but it is no longer the whole post-training story. The V4 recipe combines SFT, domain-specific GRPO and on-policy distillation into a staged pipeline.

Source cited: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence, DeepSeek-AI, arXiv, April 26, 2026

#9923. Europe's Supermarket Cyberattacks Expose a Bigger Problem With Connected Infrastructure

Associate Professor at University of Calabria. Researching LLMs, trustworthy AI, and data science. Writing on AI, tech, and society.

Associate Professor at University of Calabria. Researching LLMs, trustworthy AI, and data science. Writing on AI, tech, and society.

Associate Professor at University of Calabria. Researching LLMs, trustworthy AI, and data science. Writing on AI, tech, and society.

In recent weeks, many European supermarkets have discovered that a cyberattack can turn a refrigerator into a source of heat. Modern refrigeration systems use an automatic defrost cycle that periodically suspends cooling and heats certain components to remove ice from the coils, ensuring that the system operates properly. This process can also be controlled remotely. On the night of October 11–12, hundreds of French supermarkets were targeted by cyberattacks that manipulated refrigeration controls, extending defrost cycles and causing substantial food losses. At one Intermarché store in Gradignan, the owner reported that the temperature in a cold room had reached 50°C. On November 2, Reuters documented a new wave of incidents affecting supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, and other European countries, including another reported case of freezers reaching 50°C in Stockholm. Refrigeration incidents were also reported in Ireland, while Italian authorities confirmed that a limited number of stores had been affected.

In a previous article published on HackerNoon, titled Houston, We Have a Problem: Artificial Intelligence Is Becoming Harder to Control, we had already pointed to a particularly dangerous combination. Over the years, we have connected a growing number of systems to the Internet, often prioritizing convenience and cost savings over security. Controlling equipment remotely avoids costly on-site visits and allows for quick intervention, but it also exposes the system to potential attacks. This growing connectivity is not always matched by adequate security measures: some systems may run outdated software, use default passwords that have never been changed, rely on devices that manufacturers no longer update, or expose services directly to the Internet without sufficient safeguards. And hospitals, transportation, power grids, and other essential services now depend on these infrastructures. Meanwhile, we are developing increasingly powerful AI systems capable of writing code, using tools, and identifying vulnerabilities. So-called AI agent swarms are also emerging: groups of autonomous agents that divide tasks, work in parallel, share information, and adapt their strategies. If used maliciously, these technologies could enable attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities at speeds and on a scale that would have been unthinkable until recently. And this is where the paradox lies: as the tools for attacking grow ever more powerful, our society depends on increasingly complex digital infrastructures, often built up in a piecemeal fashion, tightly interconnected, and running software that may contain vulnerabilities.

The supermarket incidents bring an increasingly important question back into focus: if artificial intelligence is becoming such a powerful tool in the hands of attackers, why should it not be equally powerful for those defending against them? The answer lies in a fundamental feature of cybersecurity that AI may amplify: the asymmetry between attack and defense. An attacker may need to find just one vulnerability, while defenders must protect servers, applications, devices, and external connections all at once. Attackers can choose where and when to strike; defenders must be prepared for threats coming from anywhere in their infrastructure. Imagine what might happen if a hacker tasked a swarm of AI agents with autonomously exploring an infrastructure and identifying its weakest points. There is no evidence that autonomous AI agents played a role in the recent supermarket attacks, which illustrate the risks of insecure connectivity rather than AI-driven cyberattacks. The scenario is nevertheless worth considering because increasingly autonomous AI systems could make identifying and exploiting similar weaknesses faster and more scalable.

Using AI for defense, however, is far more complicated. An experiment published by Corma in August 2026 offers an interesting example. The company tested four frontier AI models in 241 attack-and-defense engagements within a controlled enterprise network. The attacking agents attempted to install persistent backdoors, while defending agents were subsequently tasked with identifying them. According to Corma, attackers established verified, reboot-surviving backdoors in 85% of engagements, whereas defenders correctly identified the planted artifacts in 22% of cases involving a verified persistent backdoor. These figures measure different outcomes and come from a specific experimental setup, rather than demonstrating a universal performance gap between offensive and defensive AI. Nevertheless, they highlight an important challenge: successfully exploiting a weakness and reliably detecting its exploitation are fundamentally different tasks.

Detecting an attack is not simply a matter of spotting unusual behavior: an authorized technician and a hacker who has stolen the technician’s credentials could issue identical commands. Moreover, attackers can afford numerous failed attempts, while defenders cannot keep shutting down essential services at every sign of suspicion. An AI system that mistakenly shut down a refrigeration unit could cause damage similar to what it was trying to prevent. Finally, even the most advanced system can only recognize threats whose signals it can observe: if those signals are not collected or interpreted correctly, the attack may go unnoticed.

The challenges of defense become even more apparent when cyberattacks have consequences in the physical world. Cyber tools have also become genuine offensive weapons in contemporary conflicts. Missiles and explosives are not necessarily needed to strike essential services: compromising power grids, hospitals, transportation, communications, or food distribution systems can cause disruption and economic losses and, in the most serious cases, put people’s lives at risk, indirectly or even directly. Of course, not every cyberattack is a military operation, but the digital domain is now an integral part of conflicts. And AI agent swarms, in some respects, resemble another technology that is changing how wars are fought: drones. Although they are very different tools, they share one important feature: they can multiply threats, putting defenders under pressure.

The war in Ukraine has shown how relatively inexpensive drones can be deployed in large numbers, forcing defenders to spend far more to intercept them. A sophisticated interceptor missile can cost many times more than the drone it is meant to shoot down, and when attacks multiply, the economic sustainability of defense becomes a problem in its own right. That is why Ukraine also uses surprisingly simple solutions, such as protective nets installed over roads to hinder drone attacks. According to Ukraine's Ministry of Defence, more than 2,200 kilometres of frontline roads had been equipped with anti-drone protection by November 2026. It is almost a paradox: in a war dominated by highly advanced technology, relatively simple physical barriers are proving useful again. The same lesson applies to cybersecurity: the best response to a sophisticated threat is not always an even more sophisticated technology. AI can help, but we also need updated systems, segmented networks, and, where possible, a decision not to connect devices to the Internet when they do not really need it.

This leads to another question: are we sure that a more digitized society is necessarily a safer one? Some countries have long recognized the importance of maintaining alternatives to digital services. In Sweden and the Netherlands, for example, authorities explicitly recommend keeping cash available in case electronic payments are disrupted. The Swedish central bank suggests around SEK 1,000 per adult, while the Dutch central bank recommends approximately €70 per adult to prepare for a possible 72-hour disruption. In a very different context, during its June 2025 conflict with Israel, Iran severely restricted Internet access, with authorities citing concerns about the alleged misuse of communication networks for military purposes. The restrictions, which culminated in a near-total shutdown, also severely disrupted ordinary citizens' communications. These are very different situations, but they help illustrate an often-overlooked point: depending entirely on digital, interconnected technologies can, in certain circumstances, become a weakness. This does not mean going back to the past or giving up innovation, but preventing a malfunction or cyberattack from paralyzing essential services.

The issue goes far beyond protecting individual systems. Electronic payments, food distribution, transportation, energy, and communications are now closely interconnected. As the supermarket incidents show, even a limited attack can have tangible consequences for everyday life. But what would happen if a disruption affected several essential services and lasted for days? As early as 2025, the European Union adopted a strategy calling for guidelines to help citizens remain self-sufficient for at least 72 hours in an emergency. In the United Kingdom, people are advised to keep supplies of water, food, cash, and even battery-powered radios, useful when the Internet and other services are unavailable. These are general precautions intended for blackouts, natural disasters, and other emergencies as well, not just cyberattacks.

At first glance, these recommendations might seem overly cautious. But when I still read about default passwords that have never been changed, services accessible directly from the Internet without adequate protection, and machines that work perfectly well but run software their manufacturers have stopped updating, I grow concerned. The old IT mantra, “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it”, is becoming dangerous: a system can continue to work flawlessly while remaining vulnerable to attack. And my concern grows when I think about the complexity of IT infrastructures, built up over time by layering software developed by different people and companies, often using different technologies, and connecting an ever-growing number of services. Add to that cameras, sensors, and other devices sometimes purchased without sufficient checks on their security. And as we continue to make everything more connected, we are developing AI systems increasingly capable of finding and exploiting precisely these weaknesses.

All the ingredients for a perfect mess are there. Let's hope for the best.

When Threats Move at Machine Speed, Governments Still Think at Human Speed

Associate Professor at University of Calabria. Researching LLMs, trustworthy AI, and data science. Writing on AI, tech, and society.

#9922. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

#9921. AI Agent Framework Issue Response Times: OpenAI Agents SDK Closed 98% of New Issues in 30 Days, LangGraph 17%

Of the GitHub issues people opened against nine AI agent framework repositories between August 23 and October 22, 2026, OpenAI's Agents SDK closed 98.3% within 30 days. LangGraph closed 17.4%, and Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK for Python closed 1 of 54.

Star counts tell you how many people bookmarked a framework. Release tags tell you the maintainers are shipping. Neither tells you what happens when you hit a bug at 2 a.m. and file an issue. So the research question was: for issues filed in the same 60-day window, how fast does each major Python agent framework close them, and how many does it close at all?

I pulled 3,562 human-filed issues on November 21, 2026. Every number below comes from the GitHub API and can be reproduced with the two-line query further down.

I took one cohort of issues per repository, all opened in the same 60-day window, and checked their state on November 21.

OpenAI's Agents SDK, then Mastra. No other repo in the sample closed even half its new issues within a week.

Issues created 2026-08-23 to 2026-10-22 UTC, bot authors excluded, state read 2026-11-21 05:35â€“05:50 UTC. Source: GitHub REST API.

The gap is big. A median OpenAI Agents SDK issue was closed in about 30 hours. Mastra handled 7.7 times as many issues in the same window and still closed the median one in 2.33 days. At the other end, 40.7% of the Claude Agent SDK's 54 issues were still open with zero comments on November 21. smolagents had 24.6% open with zero comments, and the archived AutoGen repository 34.4%.

No. In this sample, the two most-starred active repositories close the smallest share of issues on time.

CrewAI has 61,134 stars and closed 27.6% of its cohort within 30 days. LangGraph has 45,215 and closed 17.4%. On star momentum, LangGraph gained the most of any framework between November 5 and 12, and its live GitHub star tracker read 45,194 on November 20. The OpenAI Agents SDK, with half CrewAI's stars, closed 98.3%.

That is why the comparison of 19 open-source AI agent frameworks on aiagentsinfo.com, an independent research lab and AI agent directory, lists licence and latest tag rather than ranking by stars. Popularity brings in more issues. It does not bring in more people to triage them.

Not reliably. Release cadence and issue throughput are separate signals. This dataset shows them pointing in opposite directions for two vendor SDKs.

The AI agent frameworks outlook for November 2026 to May 2027 framed the six-month question this way: "which framework is still shipping, not which one will win." Its November 12 read found stable tags from the previous eight days for Pydantic AI, CrewAI, the Claude Agent SDK, Google ADK and Microsoft Agent Framework. The OpenAI Agents SDK's newest stable tag was v0.24.0, 28 days old.

The repo with the stalest stable tag had the best issue throughput, and one with a three-day-old tag had the worst. Neither number replaces the other. A framework can ship weekly from an internal roadmap while public issues pile up, or close issues fast while the stable line waits for a big runtime change (the report notes the SDK's v0.24.0-alpha.7 prerelease). If you depend on maintainers responding to your bug reports, add issue throughput to "still shipping." The release cadence study of 24 frameworks is the other half of that check.

It tells you whether "closed" means a maintainer acted or the issue timed out. For CrewAI and LangGraph, about half or more of closures are "not planned."

65.7% of CrewAI's closed issues carry state_reason: not_planned, and so do 50.6% of LangGraph's. For Mastra it is 3.5%, and for Google ADK 6.4%. I sampled eight closed issues per repo and read closed_by. Two of CrewAI's eight were closed by github-actions[bot], a stale-issue workflow. All eight sampled LangGraph closures came from one account, and five of them were "not planned." Every sampled OpenAI and Mastra closure came from a human (User) account and was marked completed. Eight is a small sample, so read it as a direction, not a rate.

This changes how CrewAI's 70.9% "closed now" should be read. Its cohort median is 36.73 days. Of its 332 closed issues, 203 were closed after day 30, and 65.7% of all closures are "not planned."

Treat it as one column next to licence, release tag and total cost, and rerun the query on the exact repo you plan to pin.

The cost side matters too. The LangGraph vs CrewAI vs OpenAI Agents SDK breakdown shows all three are MIT, and the real bills are observability seats, hosted executions and model APIs. Here is the query to reproduce any row:

For the same 60-day window, the share of new issues closed within 30 days ran from 98.3% (OpenAI Agents SDK) down to 1.9% (Claude Agent SDK for Python). Neither stars nor release cadence predicted it. Look at a repo's issue throughput and its not_planned share before you commit to it.

Data: GitHub REST API (search/issues and repos), collected November 21, 2026, 05:35â€“05:50 UTC.

#9920. For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

In this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

After those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually showed greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, showed no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”

There’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups showed improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

The takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick

In the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them new to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.)

What did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators showed greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

But that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups showed similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

So if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

If you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out.   Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

After two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another showed that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

Why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

The benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

Imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were new to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

For beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

But do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

The idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, big-picture insights.

When researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits.   So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

Using animal characters, educators can help children navigate big feelings with mindfulness and self-compassion.

A study of 38,000 people around the world finds that people who feel connected to nature are more hopeful, purposeful and resilient.

Whether we’ve been trying to improve our exercise, eating, sleep, or happiness, self-reflection is one of the most practical tools we have.

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

Psychologist and meditation teacher Tara Brach explores how practicing kindness and compassion can strengthen our relationships, ease loneliness, and help us feel more connected to others.
