#9919. CertiK and Columbia University Bring Math Proofs to the GPU Code Behind Every Large AI Model

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta plan to spend about $725 billion on capital projects in 2026, most of it on AI data centers and chips, while the cost of the largest AI training runs has grown about 2.4 times a year since 2016 and is on track to pass $1 billion by 2027. Nearly all of that money turns into time on graphics processing units (GPUs). Every second of that time runs through kernels, the small, heavily tuned programs that tell a GPU how to multiply large tables of numbers or how to compute attention, the step that lets a language model weigh every word against every other word.

Those kernels are some of the most valuable code in AI and some of the hardest to check. A bug in one rarely crashes anything, so the job keeps running while quietly producing wrong numbers that flow into the next step of training or into the answers a model gives. CertiK and researchers at Columbia University have now built TensorLean, a system that uses mathematics to prove a production GPU kernel computes what it should. The team has applied it to more than 100 kernels from DeepSeek and the widely used FlashAttention library, finding 25 bugs along the way.

The 2026 plans are large at every company. Amazon expects to approach $200 billion, Microsoft has guided to $190 billion for the calendar year, Alphabet to between $180 billion and $190 billion and Meta to between $125 billion and $145 billion, while Alphabet has already told investors that its spending will rise significantly again in 2027. Hardware such as chips, servers and the networking between them makes up 47% to 67% of the cost of developing a frontier model, so the efficiency of that hardware is where most of the money is won or lost.

That efficiency is decided by kernels. FlashAttention, the open-source attention library with more than 25,000 stars on GitHub, supplies features used in models such as Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 and Grok, while DeepSeek released kernels such as DeepGEMM, which reaches up to 1,550 trillion operations a second on an H800 GPU. Because a training cluster runs the same few kernels billions of times, a small speed gain in one of them is worth more than almost any other software change, which is why some of the best engineers in AI spend their careers making kernels faster.

The TensorLean team puts the stakes in simple terms. If a training run spends $100 million on compute and 1% of that work must be repeated because of an error, the extra cost is $1 million. At the $1 billion scale Epoch AI expects the largest runs to reach by 2027, the same 1% would cost $10 million (our arithmetic). Failures are already routine at that scale: Meta's Llama 3 405B run on 16,384 H100 GPUs saw 419 unexpected interruptions over 54 days, about one every 3.1 hours.

The failures that crash a job are the easy ones, since the job stops and restarts from a saved checkpoint. The hard ones are silent: Meta traced six interruptions in a 54-day window to silent data corruption, where a chip returns a wrong answer without any error, while Google has estimated one such event every one to two weeks during Gemini training. Researchers at Harvard and Amazon found that a model's loss curve, the main health signal engineers watch, can look normal while its weights drift away from where they should be. A bug in a kernel behaves like silent corruption with one difference that makes it costlier, because a faulty chip affects one machine while a faulty kernel is copied to every GPU that runs it.

FlashAttention shows how quickly the code has changed. The second version ran at about 350 trillion operations a second on Nvidia's H100, around 35% of the chip's peak, before FlashAttention-3 reached 740 trillion in July 2024, about 75% of peak, with close to 1.2 quadrillion using 8-bit numbers. FlashAttention-4 then reached 1,613 trillion operations a second on Nvidia's newer B200 in March 2026, a 4.6-fold rise in under three years across two chip generations.

Each jump came from a trick that makes the code harder to reason about. The kernels copy data while doing math at the same time, assign some groups of GPU threads only to loading data while others only compute, change how they split the work depending on the size of the input and use lower-precision numbers such as FP8, which doubles speed but adds rounding. Testing checks a kernel on the inputs someone thought to try, so a bug that only appears for one unusual input size, or only when a copy finishes a moment late, can pass every test and still ship.

Formal verification replaces examples with proof. A tester runs a program on chosen inputs and checks the outputs, while a formal proof shows mathematically that the program meets its requirements for every input inside a defined range. TensorLean writes these proofs in Lean, a proof language in which a small, trusted checker confirms every step, so anyone can rerun the check and get the same answer without trusting the people who wrote the proof.

The system works on PTX, the low-level instruction set Nvidia's compiler produces just before code runs on a GPU, so the proof covers the code that actually executes after the compiler has made its changes. TensorLean models the speed tricks together, including data transfers that overlap with computation, layouts that change with the size of the task and lower-precision arithmetic held to set numerical tolerances.

Specifications written for one kernel can be reused for related kernels, which lets the approach spread to more code and repeat each time that code changes. That reuse is what makes the method practical for teams that ship new optimizations every few weeks.

The team has applied TensorLean to more than 100 production GPU kernels across several generations of GPU architecture, including kernels from DeepSeek and from FlashAttention. The work uncovered two bugs in DeepSeek's kernels and 23 in FlashAttention. When a proof fails, it points to the case that breaks. Once the code is repaired, the team proves the new version again so the fix is confirmed to meet its requirements.

The choice of targets matters because both codebases are shared. FlashAttention has more than 3,000 forks on GitHub while DeepSeek's kernels were released openly for anyone to build on, which means a bug in either one travels into many other projects. A fix proved at the source protects every team downstream, which turns one research effort into a gain for a large part of the open-source AI stack.

For teams that train or serve large models, TensorLean fits into the work they already do. After each round of optimization an engineer can measure the speed gain, rerun verification to check that the change did not introduce a computational error and, when the code meets its requirements, keep a machine-checkable proof alongside it. That record lowers the risk of wasted compute, costly training reruns and wrong results feeding into later calculations, which are the losses that grow with every increase in cluster size.

The need will grow as AI writes more of its own code. Researchers are already using language-model agents to generate GPU kernels and prove them correct in Lean. Kernel code produced that way will arrive faster than any human team can review it. The practical starting point is the code that runs most often, such as attention, matrix multiplication and mixture-of-experts routing, where a proof protects the largest share of compute and where specifications can be reused across versions.

Formal verification has a long history in systems software. seL4 became the first fully verified operating system kernel in 2009. CertiKOS, a verified concurrent operating system kernel, followed at Yale with Ronghui Gu as a lead designer. Gu and Yale professor Zhong Shao founded CertiK in 2017. The company has since worked with more than 5,500 enterprise and institutional clients and found more than 119,000 code vulnerabilities.

AI has made proofs far cheaper to produce. DeepMind's AlphaProof reached silver-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad in 2024 with proofs written in Lean, while Anthropic formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean with Claude in 11 days in September, producing about 13 million lines. In October, Claude worked with the firm Theorem to prove 123 open-source libraries free of crashes with about 180 million lines of proof, roughly 900 times the size of the seL4 proof (our arithmetic). TensorLean carries that progress into the computing code that AI itself runs on.

As training budgets head toward $1 billion per run, a proof of correctness is likely to become as routine a part of shipping a kernel as a speed benchmark is today. Teams that can prove each optimization correct can push for speed with more confidence, while teams that rely on testing alone carry a growing risk of finding errors only after the compute has been spent.

For CertiK, TensorLean extends formal verification from blockchains and operating systems into AI infrastructure, the fastest-growing category of computing spend. The next test is adoption: whether the labs and library maintainers who write the fastest kernels start shipping proofs alongside them, which would give the industry a firmer base for every gain in AI computing efficiency that follows.

#9918. SC-500: The Exam That Replaced AZ-500 — Cloud Security, Now With AI Workloads on the Syllabus

AZ-500 retired on August 31, 2026. Its replacement is not a refresh with a new code: SC-500, Implementing End-to-End Security Controls for Cloud and AI Workloads, earns a differently named certification — Microsoft Certified: Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate — and it tests a job that is visibly wider than the one AZ-500 tested. The old exam asked whether you could secure Azure. SC-500 asks whether you can secure Azure, the data and networks around it, and the AI workloads running on top of it.

That last clause is the whole story. Microsoft's study guide puts AI security in two places at once: securing AI solutions sits inside the compute domain, and securing AI workloads sits inside the posture domain. A candidate who studies SC-500 as "AZ-500 with a new name" will walk into questions about Copilot data exposure, AI gateways, and agent identities that no AZ-500 material ever covered.

SC-500 certifies a security engineer who protects organizational systems and data across cloud and hybrid environments — identity, network, application, data, and compute — and who also makes sure the platforms, data, identities, and infrastructure used by AI workloads are securely implemented and monitored. That is Microsoft's audience profile, and it is deliberately broad: the exam expects you to work across Entra ID, Azure networking, storage and databases, compute, Defender, Sentinel, and Purview, and to talk to the architects, administrators, and developers who own each piece.

The exam mechanics, from Microsoft's official study guide and exam page: 120 minutes, pass mark 700 on a 1,000-point scaled score, $165 in the United States with pricing set by country or region, booked and sat through Pearson VUE at a test center or online with OnVUE proctoring. Microsoft does not publish an exact question count — most of its role-based exams run 40 to 60 — and there are no formal prerequisites, though the exam plainly assumes hands-on Azure experience. The certification is valid for one year and renews free with an online assessment on Microsoft Learn. The beta opened in May 2026 and the exam went generally available in July 2026; AZ-500 and the Azure Security Engineer Associate certification retired August 31, 2026, with no conversion path — existing AZ-500 certifications stay Active until their one-year expiry, then become Historical.

Microsoft's study guide lists four domains with a strikingly flat spread:

No domain falls below 20 percent and the largest tops out at 30. That flatness is the exam's defining structural fact: there is no light domain to skim and no single heavy domain to carry your score. Every domain is roughly a quarter of the exam, so a weak domain costs you roughly a quarter of the exam.

Identity is the control plane for everything else on this exam, and the domain tests it as an engineering discipline, not a vocabulary list. Entra ID work covers privileged identity management, conditional access, multifactor and passwordless authentication, app registrations and OAuth consent, and managed identities. Then Key Vault end to end — keys, secrets, and certificates, and the access policies that decide who can touch them. Then governance: Azure Policy, regulatory compliance in Defender for Cloud, resource locks, role-based access control including custom roles, and the unglamorous work of finding overprivileged access and removing it.

The exam's favorite trap in this domain is the difference between a control that exists and a control that is enforced. A conditional access policy in report-only mode, a PIM role that is eligible but never activated, a Key Vault access policy that grants more than the workload needs — SC-500 writes scenarios around controls that look right in the portal and fail in practice. Study the enforcement state, not the configuration screen.

A second trap is scope. Conditional access, access reviews, and entitlement management all fail the same way: applied to the wrong population. The scenario names a group of users, a set of apps, or a class of resources; the correct answer is the policy that covers exactly that scope, not the broader one that looks safer.

The heaviest domain, and the most sprawling. Storage account security and firewall rules, Defender for Storage, Azure SQL platform security and auditing, Defender for Databases — then networking: network security groups and application security groups, Azure Virtual Network Manager, Virtual WAN, VPN, Entra Private Access, private endpoints and Private Link, Azure Firewall, and Network Watcher.

Two ideas organize the whole domain. The first is defense in depth across the data path: encryption at rest and in transit, access controls on the storage account, firewall rules that admit only the right networks, and private connectivity that keeps traffic off the public internet. The exam tests the layers together — a question that is really about which layer failed, with each wrong answer fixing a different, innocent layer.

The second is that networking questions on SC-500 are connectivity questions first and firewall questions second. A scenario about a hybrid workload that cannot reach a database, a private endpoint that resolves to the wrong address, a Virtual WAN hub that routes around the firewall — the answer is usually about how traffic flows, not about which rule to add. If your study has been entirely rule-based, spend time tracing packets through NSGs, route tables, Private Link, and Firewall before exam day.

Compute covers serverless and platform services, managed identities and service principals, virtual machines and containers: hardening operating systems and workloads, securing container environments and orchestration, and managing updates and vulnerability remediation. That is the traditional half of the domain. The new half is security for AI, and it is where SC-500 most differs from AZ-500.

The AI content, per Microsoft's study guide and the exam's syllabus: data overexposure in SharePoint as it feeds Copilot, Copilot and AI app risk through Purview Data Security Posture Management, real-time protection for Copilot Studio agents, conditional access for Entra Agent ID, blast-radius analysis in Defender XDR, the AI Gateway in API Management for Microsoft Foundry, Defender for AI Service, and guardrails in Foundry. The exam treats AI workloads as ordinary workloads with extraordinary data access: an agent that can read SharePoint inherits SharePoint's exposure, and a model gateway that has no guardrails is a data path with no firewall.

The study implication is practical: if you have never opened Purview's DSPM for AI or configured an AI Gateway, do it in a trial tenant before the exam. The questions are written for people who have seen these blades, and the distractors are written for people who have only read the definitions.

The operational domain, and the second home of the AI work. It covers securing AI workloads and solutions — enforcing responsible AI and data protection, monitoring and mitigating AI-specific risks, implementing security controls for generative AI and AI platforms — alongside the posture work: assessing compliance and security posture, using Defender and Sentinel for threat detection, and responding to and remediating security incidents.

This is the domain where the exam tests judgment under pressure. The scenario gives you an alert or a posture finding, and the question is what you do first: which signal confirms the scope, which Defender or Sentinel view answers the question, when a finding is a misconfiguration to remediate and when it is an incident to escalate. The wrong answers are always real actions in the wrong order. The only reliable defense is having done the workflow once in a trial tenant: trigger an alert, open it in Defender XDR, pivot to Sentinel, check the posture score, and close it out.

The certification changed its name for a reason. AZ-500 certified an Azure Security Engineer; SC-500 certifies a Cloud and AI Security Engineer. The identity, storage, networking, and compute fundamentals carry over — Entra ID, Key Vault, NSGs, Azure Firewall, Defender for Cloud, and the rest are still the core of the job — but the exam adds AI workload security as a first-class topic in two domains, widens the networking scope toward hybrid and multi-cloud connectivity, and frames the whole job around end-to-end controls rather than Azure-only controls.

If you hold AZ-500-era study notes, audit them against the four SC-500 domains before you trust them. Anything about Entra ID, Key Vault, storage, networking, and compute fundamentals still applies. Anything that never mentions AI workloads, DSPM for AI, agent identities, or AI gateways is incomplete for this exam — and anything that describes AZ-500 as bookable is out of date. Book SC-500, not the retired exam.

Six to eight weeks suits most people who already administer Azure. The even weighting makes the plan simple: give each domain roughly equal time, and keep the last week for timed practice. A plan that front-loads identity and squeezes posture into the final days is planning to lose a quarter of the exam.

Weeks 1–2, identity and governance: PIM, conditional access, Key Vault, Azure Policy, access reviews. Build each control in a trial tenant and then try to break it — a policy in report-only mode, an overprivileged role, a vault with a loose access policy. Weeks 3–4, storage, databases, and networking: storage firewalls, SQL auditing, NSGs, Private Link, Azure Firewall, and one full connectivity trace from a hybrid workload to a database. Weeks 5–6, compute and AI: container hardening, managed identities, then the AI controls — DSPM for AI in Purview, an AI Gateway, an agent identity with conditional access. Weeks 7–8, timed runs: full 120-minute blocks under exam conditions, reading the explanation for every miss — not just the wrong answers, but the right ones you guessed.

Two habits separate passing candidates from failing ones on this exam. First, verify everything in the portals, not in a book: SC-500 tests the consoles as they are now, and the blades move. Second, practice the scenario format: read the question, name the domain, name the tool, and only then look at the options. The exam's distractors are built for candidates who match keywords to answers; the domain-first habit defeats them.

SC-500 is AZ-500's job grown wider: the same cloud security engineering, plus the AI workloads that now sit on top of it, tested across four domains that are each worth about a quarter of the exam. The flat weighting is the warning — there is nowhere to hide, and the AI content in the compute and posture domains is the part older material cannot teach you. Study the outline as it stands today, build the AI controls in a trial tenant, and practice the operational workflows as procedures, not definitions.

Start by finding out where you stand: the free SC-500 practice test at https://study4pass.com/study-material/microsoft/sc-500 runs real exam-style questions with full explanations and no signup, so you can measure each of the four domains before you commit your study weeks.

#9917. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

#9916. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9913. How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds. The power of that little “Ask anything” AI prompt box is immense, but can it help us make wiser decisions? Cheryl Strauss Einhorn, author of The Human Edge: Smarter Decisions in the Age of AI, writes:

AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it. It can illuminate pathways we might not have seen or narrow our choices in ways we do not fully recognize. As AI systems become more integrated into our lives, the challenge is no longer simply about harnessing their power but about leading them with clarity, discernment, and commitment to human agency.

She argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important. We spoke with her about why human judgment is a competitive advantage, how to engage our values when we prompt AI, and how AI can help us clarify our thinking.

Kia Afcari: You argue that AI makes human judgment more, not less, important. How can we make sure that the values of kindness and care are reflected when we use AI to help us make decisions?

Cheryl Strauss Einhorn: AI has no values. It has biases and influences by those who have designed it, and from whatever information has been fed into it. So to be sure that prosocial values are reflected when we use AI, we humans need to bring them into the work that we do together.

When working with an AI tool, we want to be asking ourselves, What is the problem that I’m solving? Why am I solving it? What is the context? And so we really need to be intentional with AI, because without asking ourselves those things first, AI doesn’t know why we’re coming to it.

Before you actually sit down with a tool, you can muster those values and those important factors related to the problem that you’re solving, and then articulate them and communicate them to the machine.

If we let the machine think for us, we can lose that sense of right and wrong, for example, because we actually care about all of those details that AI can’t possibly know about the problems that we’re solving and the people that we’re solving those problems with and for.

For example, you might ask yourself or your AI tool: Before I act, help me think through the people, relationships, and responsibilities this decision affects—not just the outcome it produces.

This type of human-centric AI interaction helped Felice, a food scientist at a pet food company, who was responsible for developing new recipes that balance nutrition, taste, and market trends. She often has to delegate tasks within her research team, ensuring that product testing, ingredient sourcing, and regulatory compliance all move forward smoothly. Using AI, she was able to analyze workloads and expertise that suggested the best person for each task, but only Felice understood the deeper dynamics at play—who works best under tight deadlines, who has a passion for innovative formulations, and who needs mentorship. When AI recommended assigning a crucial stability test to her most experienced technician, this prompt supported her thinking about a different option: giving it to the junior scientist who was eager to develop his skills in quality assurance. The AI tool’s choices made sense based on efficiency, but Felice’s decision ensured both short-term success and long-term team development.

KA: In the book, your “cheetah” metaphor celebrates slowing down. Why is a strategic pause so important when working with AI?

CSE: The cheetah metaphor relates that although this is an animal that goes zero to 60 in about three seconds, its hunting prowess actually comes from being able to decelerate up to nine miles an hour in a single stride. And the reason why that’s so important in problem solving and decision making is that’s where you build agility, flexibility, and maneuverability. Do I want to stay the course, or do I want to pivot and do something else?

This pause allows you to chunk your learning and pry open that cognitive space for new information and insight. With an AI tool, it’s so important because there’s a difference between speed and quality.

When something truly matters to us, we want to make sure that we’re solving the problem in a way that solves it holistically, that takes care of the people who are involved in the problem with us. And when we’re moving really quickly, sometimes those very important factors are hard to bring forward. So there’s a real difference between what is efficient and what is effective.

KA: Why can having more information make it harder—not easier—to make good decisions?

CSE: Francis Bacon once said, “Knowledge is power,” but that’s not really true anymore, right? We now have all of the answers with AI to a lot of commonly asked questions and some uncommon questions.

We need to make sure we’re defining the problem that we’re solving, that we are understanding and communicating the motivation and providing the context, because you don’t want all the information. Otherwise, we’re going to end up with analysis paralysis.

One thing people can use is what I call the “vision of success” question. This question asks you to time travel, to jump over the decision to see that the decision has been made well. What’s happening? What are those few things that if they don’t succeed, the decision fails? It’s actually very powerful, because it allows you to clearly identify so that you can articulate those factors that you absolutely need to be able to share with AI. These become the constraints and boundaries that set the perimeter around the decision, so that it can give you research that’s targeted and focused on those things.

For example, Max deciding where to spend his next vacation. Asking AI for help directly—without turning to himself first—he got a list of destinations, airline options, and local attractions, complete with ratings, reviews, and price comparisons. On paper, that sounds ideal. But in reality, Max quickly found himself paralyzed by the sheer amount of information. What if he picked a less-than-perfect hotel? What if he overlooked a hidden gem? AI has handed him a mountain of data, but it didn’t necessarily make the decision any easier.

However, when he used the “vision of success” question, he was able to realize and to share with his AI tool: “I want to return home feeling genuinely rested, having spent quality time with my family, without overspending or feeling like I missed the experience I was hoping for.”

Only then does AI have a meaningful problem to solve. Instead of searching for the “best” vacation—a question with no objective answer—it can help Max find the destination most likely to produce the outcome he actually wants. AI can’t define success but it can optimize for the success you define.

KA: How does the AREA method help people make wiser decisions, especially when AI is involved?   CSE: AREA is more than an acronym—it’s a framework for challenging our assumptions and thinking mistakes, and actively includes the perspectives of others. It stands for Absolute, Relative, Exploration and Exploitation, and Analysis.

The first “A,” Absolute, focuses on primary, unfiltered information straight from primary sources. “R,” Relative, shifts to external viewpoints—secondary sources connected to the subject. “E,” Exploration and Exploitation, fuels creativity: Exploration broadens research through interviews and unconventional sources, while Exploitation turns inward, challenging personal biases and assumptions. The final “A,” Analysis, synthesizes everything, bringing clarity and structure to complex decisions.

When using AI, a system like AREA becomes even more important because AI doesn’t eliminate bias—it can reflect and sometimes amplify biases in its training data, design, and the way we use it. Good decisions require a process that helps us recognize and challenge both AI’s biases and our own.

For AI, so much of the information, for example, is from Reddit. Information can be incomplete or outdated, and you also know that you’re interacting with a liar. It’s a machine that just gives you answers that are wrong sometimes.

So you need to be able to have a quality due diligence process to not only be able to use the tool effectively, but to be able to evaluate its outcome. Too often, people look at an answer with AI and think that it’s a transaction, and they can just take it. AREA is going to help you make sure that it’s a conversation. So you have an evidence-based perspective that has looked at a variety of stakeholder viewpoints, and made sure that you have pried open that cognitive space to challenge the natural, well-worn mental pathways that we all lean on every day.

KA: How can we use AI in ways that strengthen—rather than undermine—our values and agency?

CSE: It’s a great question. I think the new competitive advantage is going to be self-awareness.

This is the first tool that actually asks for some of our cognitive load; it wants us to offload some of our decisions to it. And this is a machine fundamentally about decision making, because we ask it for something and it gives us an answer. But there’s a very interesting invitation here, which is to each of us to get to know ourselves better.

We each have a special sauce, which is the way that we make our decisions, and we make thousands of them every single day. But most of us have not sat down and said to themselves, What does that process actually look like? Can I actually name those pieces and put language to it?

There is this invitation to get to know our thinking so that we can translate it better, and not only for the tool. How helpful would it be in conversation with our colleagues to be able to say clearly, This is how I’m actually going through the steps, this is how I’m thinking about it, these are the variables that I’m prioritizing, and here’s what I think is the most diagnostic.

You can think about your thinking skills as muscles. If we turn over our cognitive load, we will also weaken it. But if we actually take this invitation to understand our self-awareness and our metacognition, we can make sure that we strengthen those tools.

AI is a tool that has so many implications for our environment and for our world, in addition to the fact that it has implications for our actual thinking skills.

So I would say that the invitation is to turn to yourself first. Ask yourself why you’re using the tool, and whether or not you should be turning to yourself instead. And either way, bring your own thinking forward before sitting down, so that you can feel far more comfortable that you can problem-solve both with it and beyond it.

#9911. Jira: See Who Deleted an Issue in the Audit Log

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at leanzero.net

To see who deleted a Jira issue in Jira Cloud (Atlassian now calls issues "work items" and projects "spaces"), open Settings > System > Audit log and type the work item key, or "Deleted Jira issue", in the search box. The entry names the user and the time. You need the Administer Jira global permission, and at least one of your Jira apps has to be on a paid plan. I'll use Atlassian's new words from here on.

That entry is fairly new in Cloud. Atlassian closed the request for it, JRACLOUD-59371, on 16 February 2025, after nine years and 746 votes. Before that, Community answers for Cloud said no, correctly at the time. A Community Champion wrote in January 2024, in the thread Can I view a deleted issue and see who did it in Jira Software?, that "Cloud doesn't log the Jira issue delete". Plenty of those older answers still rank, which is why the question keeps coming back.

So on 21 November 2026 we ran a test on our own test site. We created 23 work items in a throwaway space and deleted 8 of them through five different routes: the work item menu, the REST API, a parent with its sub-task, a bulk call and an automation rule. All 8 showed up in the site audit log. Then we moved the space, with its last 15 work items, to trash and restored it. They all came back.

The log answers who and when. It can't tell you what the work item said, because it keeps only the key, and it can't bring the work item back. It also forgets. Six months is the most it keeps.

Before you start. Role: a Jira admin (the Administer Jira global permission). Plan: any paid Jira Cloud plan; the log isn't there if every Jira app on the site is on Free. This is Jira Cloud; the Data Center route is further down. When you're done you'll have the name of the person or app that deleted the work item and the minute it happened.

You should see a row with "Deleted Jira issue" under Change summary and the key under Changed object. If you see nothing, check the date against your retention setting (it's further down): an entry older than that is gone.

You can get the same records from the REST API with GET /rest/api/3/auditing/record and the same Administer Jira permission, which is handy if you want them in a spreadsheet or a ticket. A delete record from our test held an id, the summary "Deleted Jira issue", the category "issue", the author's account ID and the time. Its eventSource was empty. The only part about the work item was objectItem: the key and the type ISSUE_DELETE.

Atlassian's Data Center article warns that some of its methods only catch deletes made with the Delete button, and it says nothing about Cloud paths. So we tried each path in our throwaway space, AUDT, and read the log after each delete.

An API token acts as the person who created it, so a script running on someone's token shows that person's name. If your team runs a script on one admin's token, the script's deletions look like that admin's.

For the automation row you need a second step. "Automation for Jira" tells you a rule did it, but not which rule or who built it. You'd go to the space's automation settings (or global automation, for a rule that runs across spaces) and read each rule's audit log for that minute. We didn't do that part in this test.

We used the REST bulk endpoint for the bulk test and not the Bulk change screen in Jira, so that one path is the API version.

On our Premium site, the delete dialog asks "Delete or archive AUDT-1?", says "Deleting is irreversible. It permanently removes the work item, comments and attachments", and won't enable the Delete button until you type the word "delete".

Archiving hides the work item from the space but keeps it, so you can restore it later from the space's list of archived work items if someone changes their mind. Atlassian's product manager pointed people to it in the JRACLOUD-59371 thread, as a Premium and Enterprise feature. Archiving doesn't appear in the site audit log, though: we archived AUDT-15 and restored it four seconds later, and the log had nothing for either step. The work item's change history, which we read through the REST API, recorded both.

There are two audit logs, and a lot of the confusion online comes from mixing them up.

The site audit log is the one above: Jira settings, any paid plan, Jira admins. Atlassian's page Audit activities in Jira says it "will show a deletion event, including the user who performed the deletion and the date and time". It also says it "isn't intended to record all activity in Jira".

The organization audit log lives in Atlassian Administration (admin.atlassian.com) under Insights, for organization admins. Atlassian's top search result, How to find which user deleted a Jira issue, points Cloud readers only there and says "Atlassian Guard Premium or Cloud Enterprise licenses may be required". That article is marked Data Center only, and it doesn't cover the site log.

Atlassian's own pages disagree about which plans see Jira user activity, such as "Deleted Jira issue", in the organization log. The audit log activities page gives the Jira "App user log" to Cloud Enterprise and Guard Premium only. The Guard plan availability page ticks Guard Standard for "Audit logs for user activities", though. Guard Standard is listed at $4.35 per user per month and Premium at $8.55 on Atlassian's Guard pricing page (the 100-user figures). If you're on Guard Standard, open the organization log and search for a key you know was deleted before you rely on it. We didn't read our own organization log for this test.

For the question "who deleted this work item", I think the site log is enough, and paid sites already have it. You'd probably want the organization log only if you need a year of history or one log across Jira and Confluence.

Under Audit log > Actions > Audit Log Settings, the Retention period list offers exactly three choices: 1 month, 3 months and 6 months. You pick one and select Save. Our site was on 3 months, and the oldest entry we could read on 21 November was from 24 August 2026. Atlassian's page only says "e.g. 6 months", so I can't tell you whether 3 months is the default or a value someone on our side picked earlier.

Six months is the ceiling, and the request to raise it, JRACLOUD-68267, has 233 votes and the status Gathering Interest. If an auditor asks for more than 6 months of evidence, you have two native ways to keep it. First, export the log every month. The Export button saves up to 100,000 events as a CSV file; past that, it keeps the newest. It also ignores any filter you typed.

Second, there's the organization audit log with Guard. Atlassian says that from 1 October 2026 it keeps 365 days of activity. Its CSV export is capped at 10,000 activities from the past 180 days, though.

Once an entry passes the window it's gone for good. For the organization log, Atlassian adds that upgrading your plan later "doesn't recover events from before you upgraded".

The Jira site audit log doesn't record a deleted comment or a deleted attachment, and Atlassian's category table for it has no row for either. (In service spaces, Atlassian says work item and attachment activity is also shared with the Jira Service Management audit log, in beta since October 2026, under Settings > Jira Service Management > Audit log. We didn't check it.) On 21 November we added a comment to AUDT-9 and deleted it three seconds later. On AUDT-10 we did the same with a small text file. Nothing in the audit log. The History tab under Activity on each work item had both, with the person and the minute.

This trail lives inside the work item. If someone deletes the whole work item, its History goes with it, along with every comment and attachment entry the History tab used to show you.

No. Atlassian's page says a deleted work item is "permanently removed from your Jira site" and "can't be recovered unless you have a backup or export from before the deletion". There's no recycle bin for single work items; the request for one, JRACLOUD-36415, has 722 votes and is Under Consideration.

A whole space, for 60 days. Moving a space to trash keeps it, with its work items, for that long. We trashed AUDT and restored it, and all 15 work items left in it came back. The audit log recorded "Project marked as deleted" and "Deleted project restored", each with the space name.

An archived work item. You restore it from Archived work items.

Anything in a backup. Atlassian Backup and Restore is a paid add-on for Premium and Enterprise plans billed annually. Atlassian's pricing page estimates $7,000 a year for Jira at 1,000 users. When it became generally available in February 2026, Atlassian's announcement described restoring "to an empty production site or sandbox". We don't have it on our test site, so we couldn't try pulling one work item back from it.

The audit log still helps with the backup route. Its key and time tell you which backup to open and which work item to look for.

Data Center has had this since Jira 8.8.0. Atlassian's Data Center article says to set Audit Logs > Settings > Coverage > End user activity to Advanced. From then on it records events such as "Issue deleted" and "Issue attachment deleted". It only works for deletions made after you change the setting. We run Cloud only, so this part comes from Atlassian's article and not from our test.

This one caught us out. Our test account is a Jira admin, so it can read the audit log. In the AUDT space we created through the REST API, it still got "403" on its first deletes, and the bulk call said "You do not have permission to delete the selected AUDT-14 issues."

Delete work items is a space permission. Being a Jira admin doesn't give it to you. AUDT used the permission scheme "Default software scheme", which grants Delete work items to two holders only: the space's Administrators role and the role apps use (atlassian-addons-project-access). Our admin wasn't in that role. We added it, and the deletes went through. Jira logged the role change too: "Project roles changed", Administrators, with the account added. So if someone adds themselves to a role and then deletes things, the log shows both steps.

Atlassian's work item permissions page also says that Delete work items removes the work item "including their associated data, even if the user doesn't have Delete all comments or Delete all attachments permissions".

If you run a Jira Cloud site with more than a handful of people deleting things, this is what I'd do, in this order:

One more option, which we haven't measured. If you want the summary of what was deleted, look at Atlassian's own knowledge base article. It shows an automation rule with the Work item deleted trigger and a Log action that writes the key and {{initiator.displayName}}. You could add {{issue.summary}} to the message. Once usage billing starts on 3 December 2026, Atlassian's usage page counts the trigger as a step each time it runs and doesn't count the Log action. It also says runs that end with no actions performed cost nothing, and it doesn't say which way a Log-only run falls. We tried to create this rule through the Automation API on our site and got a server error twice, so we haven't measured it. Our measured guide to automation steps per rule shows how to read what a rule actually costs once it runs.

If you're weighing Guard for the longer organization log, our piece on what Atlassian's data security policies need Guard for covers the plan lines, and how many Jira administrators you need is the other half of the "who can delete" question.

Has the audit log ever settled a "where did my work items go" argument for you, or did it stop at the key? Tell me in the comments or on the Atlassian Community; I'm curious how many of you already had retention on 6 months.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

#9910. Hidden preferences in VLM finetuning shift bias

Fine‑tuning a vision‑language teacher on covert objectives injects a measurable bias into its student models. The paper demonstrates that an animal‑preference signal hidden in the teacher’s finetuning data reappears after distillation, shifting downstream behavior by roughly ten percentage points. This reveals a concrete pathway for subtle fairness violations to propagate through standard VLM pipelines.

Prior work on large language models had identified hidden preference transmission, and it was not yet known whether similar subliminal bias transfer occurs in vision‑language systems. Prior studies on large language models identified hidden preference transmission, but vision‑language systems had not been examined under the same lens.

Students trained on biased‑teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to 10 percentage points in the animal preference task [1]. In one concrete evaluation the control student chose the preferred animal 30.50 % of the time while the biased student reached 40.42 %, confirming the ten‑point shift on an unrelated geometric‑shape task.

The study leaves open how far this hidden bias travels beyond the narrow geometric‑shape probe. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated [1], suggesting that larger finetuning corpora could amplify subtle preferences and that different generation strategies may modulate the effect.

Fairness pipelines that prune teacher VLMs must now audit for covert preference signals before distillation, or else downstream student models will inherit undetected biases even when evaluated on unrelated tasks.

#9909. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain.
