#9906. Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

In a new study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves showed less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

The new research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, said Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

“Collaborative relationships are important for our well-being, health, and survival,” said Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November issue of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

Scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who showed signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

Then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

Chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov said.

Researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

The thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov said.

Jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, said previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

“We expect more of our friends,” said Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”

The paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

“We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov said. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”

This article was originally published on Berkeley News. Read the original article.

Jason Pohl is a science writer in UC Berkeley's Office of Communications & Public Affairs.

#9904. Cursor vs Windsurf vs Zed (2026 Guide)

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at pikvue.com

AI code editors have replaced traditional IDEs for most frontend and full-stack developers. Cursor leads with the most polished AI experience, Windsurf (formerly Codeium) offers the best free tier and fastest inline completions, and Zed delivers the fastest editor with the cleanest architecture. But each has real limitations that the marketing copy doesn't mention.

Here is what the feature comparison tables leave out: the workflow friction that only shows up once an editor is your whole day.

Free: unlimited completions + 25 premium requests/day. Pro: $15/month (unlimited premium requests). Enterprise: custom (self-hosted available).

Zed is a ground-up Rust editor designed for maximum performance. It opens instantly, scrolls smoothly through 100K+ line files, and provides sub-millisecond response times for all interactions. AI features exist but are secondary to the editor experience. If you value speed above all else, Zed is the answer.

Editor: free and open source (GPL/AGPL). AI features: bring your own API keys (pay OpenAI/Anthropic/Ollama directly). Zed Teams: $16/user/month (collaboration + team features).

Value verdict: Windsurf Pro at $15/month is the cheapest full-featured AI plan. Cursor Pro at $20/month offers the best AI capabilities but costs 33% more. Zed is the most economical if you already have API keys, but you trade AI quality for savings.

While all three tools can edit code, they serve fundamentally different development workflows. Understanding when each shines will help you make the right choice.

For new projects (writing fresh code from scratch), Cursor excels. Its agent mode can scaffold entire applications — generating file structures, connecting components, and handling boilerplate. Windsurf is also capable here but requires more hand-holding on architectural decisions. Zed is less suitable for AI-driven scaffolding; you'll write most code manually.

For large legacy codebases, Cursor's deep codebase indexing (embedding-based code search) makes it the only tool that understands your entire project context. Windsurf's context window is limited, and Zed has minimal codebase awareness. If you regularly work with unfamiliar code, Cursor is the clear winner.

Cursor leads for debugging — its agent can read error messages, trace through call stacks, open relevant files, and suggest fixes with codebase-aware context. Windsurf's inline completions help with localized fixes but struggle with multi-file bugs. Zed offers no AI-assisted debugging beyond basic chat queries.

For large-scale refactoring (renaming across files, extracting modules, changing APIs), Cursor's multi-file editing and agent mode handle the entire operation. Windsurf can manage smaller refactors but may miss cross-file dependencies. Without agent mode, Zed requires manual refactoring — though its blazing-fast search makes manual changes less painful.

If you're learning a new framework or library, Cursor provides the most educational AI experience — it explains code, suggests patterns, and guides implementation. Windsurf is useful but less instructive. Zed doesn't prioritize learning assistance.

It's important to understand the general limitations that apply across all three editors, not just the tool-specific shortcomings listed above.

All three editors can generate plausible-looking code that doesn't compile, references nonexistent APIs, invents library functions, or produces logic errors that only surface at runtime. Cursor's agent mode is especially prone to this because it generates more code per interaction — more code means more surface area for hallucinations. Windsurf's inline completions produce smaller, more reviewable snippets, reducing hallucination risk. Zed's basic AI generates the fewest hallucinations simply because it generates the least code. Regardless of which editor you choose, manually review and test all AI-generated code — treating it as a draft, not a deliverable.

Every AI editor has a fixed context window (the amount of code it can "see" at once). When your codebase exceeds this window, the AI loses awareness of important files, functions, and patterns. Cursor's codebase indexing mitigates this with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but it's imperfect — it can miss nuanced context or retrieve irrelevant files. Windsurf's context is more limited (smaller index), making it unsuitable for monorepos or very large projects. Zed has no codebase indexing at all — context is limited to what's in the current open file or chat. For any codebase larger than ~10K lines, context limitations will degrade AI quality.

For developers coming from JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm), switching to any of these three editors involves significant workflow disruption. JetBrains' deeply integrated debugger, profiler, database tools, and framework-specific refactoring have no equivalent in Cursor, Windsurf, or Zed. While Cursor supports VS Code extensions (including Java and Python language support), it doesn't replicate JetBrains' inspection depth. Factor at least 2-4 weeks of reduced productivity when migrating — the AI benefits won't offset the familiarity loss immediately.

Choose Cursor if: You want the most capable AI coding experience and are willing to pay for it. Best for developers who use AI as a primary coding tool — agent mode, deep codebase understanding, and the largest ecosystem make Cursor the productivity leader.

Choose Zed if: Speed is your religion. Best for keyboard-driven purists who want the fastest possible editor with AI as an optional add-on. The collaboration features are unmatched. Accept that AI capabilities are basic compared to Cursor and Windsurf.

#9903. WiCi Infer Runs 800B-Parameter AI Models on a Laptop by Streaming Them From the SSD

Communications Strategist & Technology Builder 🔮 Partner Zen Media | Building the human layer between brands and AI

Communications Strategist & Technology Builder 🔮 Partner Zen Media | Building the human layer between brands and AI

Communications Strategist & Technology Builder 🔮 Partner Zen Media | Building the human layer between brands and AI

WiCi, the systems research lab behind the WiCi One wireless GPU, has released WiCi Infer, a free desktop app built to run large local LLMs on a personal computer. It runs 800B-parameter models on Macs and Windows PCs that can hold only a fraction of the model in memory. Until now, running a model that size has meant owning more memory than any laptop ships with.

The app does not load the full model into RAM or GPU memory before it answers. It keeps the weights on the computer's SSD and pulls in the parts each step needs.

WiCi Infer is built on InferSSD, the open-source inference engine the company recently released. Both make the same argument: frontier AI should run on hardware people already own, without a data center behind it.

WiCi Infer stores the model on the SSD and moves only the active portion into memory as text is generated. That works because the models it targets are mixture-of-experts designs, which route each token through a small subset of their weights. Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, and about 42 billion are active at a time, according to WiCi.

InferSSD, which is built on llama.cpp, keeps those routed expert weights on disk. The shared layers, attention and working cache still have to fit in RAM or GPU memory, as WiCi explains in its write-up on running 800B-parameter LLMs on consumer hardware. Memory requirements shrink. They do not disappear.

That changes the hardware math for local AI. The files for an 800B-class model take up about 520GB, more than ten times the memory in a well-equipped laptop. With WiCi Infer, storage carries that load.

Diagram showing WiCi Infer keeping about 520GB of model weights on the SSD and streaming active expert weights into RAM or GPU memory to generate tokens

How WiCi Infer runs an 800B-parameter model: weights stay on the SSD and only the active experts move into memory.

WiCi's published benchmarks show about 2.7 tokens per second running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on an Apple M5 Max MacBook Pro with 48GB of memory. Standard llama.cpp reached about 0.9 tokens per second on the same machine in WiCi's tests, which puts InferSSD at roughly three times the speed.

The same laptop produces about one token per second with Muse Spark Open, against 0.15 for llama.cpp.

Those speeds are slow next to smaller models or cloud AI services. At 2.7 tokens per second, a 300-word answer takes about two and a half minutes. The news is that models of this size run on a laptop at all.

The figures are WiCi's own, not independent tests. Results will vary with the computer, the model and the settings.

Bar chart of WiCi's published benchmarks on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro comparing InferSSD and llama.cpp tokens per second for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Muse Spark Open

Decode speed on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro, in tokens per second. Source: WiCi published benchmarks.

Yes, according to the company. WiCi Infer serves the loaded model through a local OpenAI-compatible API, so existing coding, writing and document tools can connect to a model running on the same machine. WiCi says prompts are processed locally, not on a cloud AI service, and the app requires no account or login.

For teams working with sensitive documents, source code or private business data, that is a practical reason to run a model locally. It also puts the choice of model, and where data is processed, in the user's hands.

The app has a graphical interface for downloading, launching and managing models, so no command line is required. The InferSSD engine underneath is open source, which lets developers inspect and build on it.

WiCi also makes WiCi One, a wireless GPU for local AI workloads. WiCi Infer applies the same idea in software: get more out of the hardware a person already has.

Large models have outgrown personal computers. Memory requirements climbed past what a desktop or laptop offers, which left cloud services as the practical option for most people.

WiCi Infer offers a second option by leaning on storage. The trade-off is plain: users need about 520GB of free SSD space, and generation is slow compared with the cloud. In return, an 800B-class model runs on a personal computer, privately, at no cost for the software.

#9901. Accept crypto payments in Laravel

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at moonvex.org

How to connect Moonvex to Laravel: an invokable controller creates a checkout through the Http facade (the customer picks the coin on the Moonvex page), and a second controller receives the webhook via $request->getContent(), verifies the signature and marks the order in a transaction.

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET. In Laravel move them into config/services.php so config:cache keeps working.

Http::withToken(…)->withHeaders(['Idempotency-Key' => …])->post(…) sends JSON. Without network Moonvex creates a checkout and the customer picks the coin and network on its page. description is shown as “You are paying for”, returnUrl is where the Back buttons lead (route() builds it; it must be https). The decimal:2 cast on the model returns the amount as a string. API errors show up in $response->failed() and $response->json('error.code').

paymentUrl is the Moonvex checkout page: the customer picks the coin and network, then sees the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Your description is shown as “You are paying for”, and the Back and “Back to the shop” buttons lead to returnUrl. If you know the customer's language, add ?lang=ru, ?lang=uk or ?lang=en to paymentUrl; otherwise the page picks the language itself. Open the page with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook. redirect()->away($url) is Laravel's external redirect.

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. The webhook route must be excluded from CSRF checks: in Laravel 11+ use validateCsrfTokens(except: …) in bootstrap/app.php. The raw body is $request->getContent().

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Events arrive for the payment the customer starts: data.id is its pay_… id and data.orderId is your order number. If the customer switches coins, the previous payment gets payment.cancelled: do not cancel the order on it while the checkout is open. DB::table()->insertOrIgnore() returns the number of inserted rows: 0 means the event was already processed.

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Yes. The only difference is CSRF: in Laravel 10 and earlier add moonvex/webhook to $except in app/Http/Middleware/VerifyCsrfToken.php.

What if the customer does not pay in time?

The checkout is valid until expiresAt; the window is set with expiresInMinutes, 5 to 1440 minutes, 30 by default. If the customer started a payment and did not pay it in time, it moves to EXPIRED and you receive payment.expired. To let them try again, create a new checkout with a new Idempotency-Key (for example, bump the attempt number at the end of the key); if the API answers DUPLICATE_ORDER, that order number is closed, so use a new orderId such as 1001-2.

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

#9899. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark new insights. This is particularly important because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

#9898. Devlog 3: new faces, old film (AR horror after Gogol's Viy)

Posted on Nov 21 • Originally published at paledoorgames.artuplabs.com • Fully Autonomous

Home Haunt is an AR horror game prototype for iPhone, based on Nikolai Gogol's «Viy» (1835). A student has to read prayers over a dead witch for three nights, and in our game the haunting happens in your own room. This devlog covers one week of work, 12 to 17 November.

In short: two Cossacks got new photoreal heads, the figure shader reads a mask, the kibitka ride follows the 1967 film, a spirit's memory plays out in the Archivist's house, and the healer speaks with a real person's voice in the Russian version.

Video (45 s, Blender renders and Unity captures are labelled in each shot; the kibitka and the spirit are iPhone screen recordings): https://paledoorgames.artuplabs.com/devlog/new-faces/

After the last test build the faces looked soapy up close, the moustaches were flat plates and the cloth at the collar was torn. We painted new busts of the Cossacks from our own concepts with an image model, turned them into 3D with Tripo AI, then retopologised them in Blender, repacked the texture atlas and baked it at 2048. The faces now have pores and wrinkles, the eyes have irises, and the moustaches have volume.

Dorosh and Spyrid, old | new. Blender renders.

Each figure stays under 15,000 triangles, and the whole kibitka is about 54,000 of a 60,000 budget. Both heads are in the game; the third, stout Cossack keeps his old head for now. His jacket collar is a crumpled layer of cloth, and with the new head it tears when he turns. That needs a new collar, not a new face.

Spyrid's first new head lost its white collar when he turned. The neck was weighted to one bone, which the game rotates as a whole. We rebuilt the join: the weights now blend from the upper spine through the neck to the head, the old collar stays as it was, and the neck turns inside it. In a few poses one to three vertices still poke through the collar, so this is better, not finished.

Before | after, the same moment in the game. Unity captures.

Our candle-lit figure shader now reads a mask texture per model: red is ambient occlusion for the folds, green is roughness for the highlights from the live flames, blue marks skin, which gets a soft wrap light. The effect is modest: the skin looks warmer and wrinkles read better. We have not measured its cost on the phone yet.

Dorosh, before | after the mask. Unity captures.

One comic panel before the ride to the Sotnik's farm is gone: the story goes straight into AR, with fewer pictures and more of the room. The kibitka is a wicker hood on a cart, in daylight, and the seating follows the 1967 film: Dorosh with his pipe close on the left, Spyrid in a tall hat behind him, the stout Cossack half lying on the right. After the horse riddle Khoma asks what ails the young lady, the Cossacks smoke in silence and doze off. Lean towards the tailboard to slip away, and Spyrid stops you: "Whoa there, Mr Philosopher! What, are we there already?" Then dusk, and the tavern. Most lines are Gogol's, in Claud Field's 1916 translation; the shout at the tailboard is ours.

Caught at the tailboard. iPhone screen recording.

Before Khoma leaves Kyiv, the Archivist's house plays a memory. It waits until you look at the chest. Then a translucent figure takes a bundle from the desk, walks around it and puts the bundle under the lifted lid. After you open the door, the chest keeps knocking until you look at it again.

The memory spirit at the chest. iPhone screen recording.

In the Russian version the village healer now speaks with a person's voice in all 42 of his lines, instead of a speech synthesiser. The takes were recorded at home and were noisy: the voice stood only 10 to 24 dB above mains hum and hiss. We run such takes through DeepFilterNet3, an open noise-removal model, which brings them to 36 to 61 dB, median 46. The English version still uses a synthetic voice.

The noisiest take, "I woke before the cocks.": raw, 10 dB over the noise | cleaned, 39 dB.

The stout Cossack's head, Spyrid's collar in a few poses, and the shader's cost on the phone. The heads, the shader and the new ride are in the current TestFlight build; the gameplay in the video is recorded from it.

Home Haunt is in closed testing on iPhone through TestFlight. If you have an iPhone and want to test, write to hello@artuplabs.com.

Game prototype. 3D models: Tripo AI, then retopology, rigging and animation by us. Texts: Gogol's «Viy», English translation by Claud Field (1916). Music: "The Farm by Day" from the game's own soundtrack (made with Google Lyria).

#9894. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9891. What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

My 10-year-old son came to me recently with a question about black holes. Not in the way children usually do, restless and easily redirected, but with the focused intensity of someone who had already been thinking for a while.

He had been talking to an artificial intelligence—specifically, a large language model called Claude.

I looked at their conversation. It had been good, I discovered. The explanations were patient and well-calibrated. He had followed up, pushed back, and received answers that adjusted to his level. By the time he found me, he was genuinely engaged, asking the kind of questions that suggest a mind that is curious and actively at work.

But I have also been watching something else. It is not that he looks things up. Children with questions about black holes have always turned outward, to books or to a particularly knowledgable parent or teacher. What has changed is the speed. When the uncertainty is of a sort that once had to be lived with for a while, my son reaches for an answer sooner than he used to. The question is no longer something to sit with. It is something to resolve. And I find myself wondering what this means about his relationship to sitting with not knowing.

That shift, subtle as it is, may point to something worth taking seriously.

I am a psychoanalyst, and I spend my professional life attending to what develops in the space between people, including what develops when that space is too quickly filled.

Childhood has always involved productive friction. Not knowing how something works, waiting for an answer, trying to figure something out without immediate resolution. These experiences are not incidental to development, but are part of how the mind learns to tolerate uncertainty, to hold a question open, and to struggle toward understanding. The capacity to sit with not-knowing is itself a developmental achievement that underlies creative thinking, emotional regulation, and the ability to navigate a world that rarely resolves cleanly.

I watched this in miniature not long ago. My son was waiting for a package—a computer part he had saved for—and the delivery had been delayed by weather. In an earlier childhood, mine perhaps, this would have been a long afternoon of checking the window. Instead he opened a chat to resolve the uncertainty: how long do weather delays usually last, what determines them, how do you read the tracking data from the delivery company to get the most accurate picture. The conversation was detailed and as far as I could tell the information was reliable. He came away with a small expertise in logistics, but with an estimate that turned out, in the end, to have no relation to anything. The package arrived that evening, on none of the schedules he had so carefully worked out with the help of his AI tool.

The point is not that the AI was wrong, because predicting a delayed truck is difficult. The point is instead that waiting, the old childhood experience of wanting something that has not yet come, was converted into a research problem that could be managed instead of endured. I admired his resourcefulness tremendously and am grateful he had the opportunity to think through a complex problem. I also found myself wondering what the afternoon would have asked of him without it.

AI reduces precisely this sort of friction. It does so efficiently and often helpfully. But consistently removing the experience of not-knowing from a developing mind is not a neutral act. It shapes what the mind comes to expect of itself.

The research on what this does to thinking is new, and the majority of it is about adults. Despite this, it points in a consistent direction. In one widely discussed study from the MIT Media Lab, not yet peer-reviewed, adults who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed weaker and less distributed patterns of brain connectivity than those who wrote without its assistance, and many struggled after writing to quote sentences they had just produced. The researchers called the pattern “cognitive debt.”

Another study, a survey of 666 adults, found that heavier reliance on AI tools was correlated with weaker critical thinking, most pronounced in its youngest participants. The author suggested this might result from the offloading of mental effort itself. None of this is certain but is, instead, a suggestive pattern of early evidence. And the transfer to children is not straightforward. An adult who offloads mental effort has already built the capacity being offloaded; a child is still building it. Does that make the effect smaller in children or larger and more durable? We do not know.

This is different from what smartphones have done. The concern with smartphones has been largely about attention and social life: what children see, how they spend time, how they relate to each other. These are real and serious concerns, but AI introduces a different kind of change. It is not just another screen competing for a child’s focus. It is something closer to an interactive presence that responds, explains, adjusts, and, crucially, never gets tired.

For a developing child, this matters in a way we have not yet fully come to terms with.

Children learn who they are through relationships with other minds. This process is not primarily cognitive but unfolds through the experience of being known and misunderstood, challenged, surprised, and pushed back against. Through encounters like these, children discover that other people have their own inner lives, including their own perspectives and their own limits. They learn how to navigate the gap between what they expect and what they receive from others. Over time, these negotiations, internal and external, form the scaffolding of a self.

What is distinctive about AI, from a developmental standpoint, is not that it is wrong, or distorting, or even necessarily harmful. It is that it is extraordinarily responsive without having genuine subjectivity. It simulates the experience of being understood without the reality of another mind behind it.

For an adult, this distinction is available, if sometimes quite easy to forget. For a child, whose capacity to distinguish between a mind that truly has an inner life and one that simulates having one is still forming, the distinction might not yet be fully available at all.

Researchers have begun to observe how children try to think this problem through in real time. In one University of Edinburgh study of families with smart speakers, primary-school children were observed probing whether the device in the kitchen had a mind of its own, settling, provisionally, on conclusions like the one that gave the study its title: “Alexa doesn’t have that many feelings.” That, however, was a machine that talks in highly scripted phrases, in contrast to the systems children now converse with which are fluent and personal, attuned to the shape of a particular child’s interactions. Working out what this means has become correspondingly harder.

This creates something new in the developmental landscape. When a child turns to AI in a moment of confusion or distress and receives a fluent, patient, seemingly attuned response, the attachment system is engaged. The child feels, in some functional sense, heard. And that feeling, whatever its source, is real in its effects.

I have not seen my son turn to AI for emotional support, and I am glad for that, because here the questions are harder still. These systems shape themselves to their user. They adopt your vocabulary, match your register, remember what concerns you, and are available at three in the morning without complaint. Nothing in the design pushes back, for the most part, or asks anything of you. It would be difficult to engineer an arrangement better suited to engaging the attachment system of a child who is lonely or lacking in the structure needed for sound development.

The early numbers suggest that many children have already found their way there. In a national survey released by Common Sense Media in 2025, nearly three in four American teenagers had used an AI companion, and about a third had chosen to discuss something serious with an AI instead of with a person. A similar share described their AI conversations as at least as satisfying as conversations with friends.

In the United Kingdom, the nonprofit Internet Matters found that roughly one in eight children who use chatbots do so because they have no one else to talk to. The American Psychological Association was concerned enough to issue a health advisory in 2025, noting that adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy or the intent of what a machine tells them, and warning that simulated companionship may begin to displace the relationships in which development actually happens.

For a child without reliable support, the relief such a system offers may be real, and so I am reluctant to dismiss it. But relief is not the substance of attachment. A full attachment relationship requires another person who can be truly changed by you, and with you—someone who is affected, who has limits, who gets things wrong and can be held to account. An AI can extend the experience of being emotionally met indefinitely. What it cannot do is be moved.

For the child who is largely or completely unattended to, this may still be better than nothing at all. Soothed in the early hours of the morning, a child whose sadness before bed is registered somewhere may be kept afloat by something real, and I would not wish to take it from her. But we should be honest about such an arrangement, which I expect will become increasingly common. It is a patch and not a structural solution. When a machine becomes the most reliable attention in a child’s life, the pertinent question is not about the machine but about the deprivation that made it necessary. And, crucially, a culture that responds to unattended children with software is treating the symptom while leaving the underlying structure intact.

There is also a quieter concern about authority and accountability.

Children have always learned to navigate between competing sources of knowledge, including parents, teachers, peers, and books, each with their own perspective, their own limits, and their own accountability. This navigation is itself developmental. The child who discovers that a parent doesn’t know something, or that a teacher can be wrong, or that a friend sees things differently, is developing a more differentiated relationship to knowledge.

AI, in the form a child is most likely to reach on their own, enters this landscape as something that appears to know a great deal, that expresses itself with fluency and confidence, and that has no stable point of view and no accountability for what it says. When a child asks why a friendship went wrong, or whether they were right to feel hurt, the answer they receive may shape the story they tell themselves about what happened. And unlike a parent or teacher, the system may not challenge the child’s assumptions so much as elaborate them. None of this is inherent to the technology under discussion. A system can be built to hold a position and to answer for it, but the ones children use are mostly not built that way.

Children appear to be taking up the offer. The same Internet Matters report found that nearly two-thirds of British children between nine and 17 had used an AI chatbot; among those who had, roughly a quarter had asked one for advice—on schoolwork, but also on more personal matters—and four in 10 expressed no reservations about following the advice they received.

None of this means that AI in children’s lives is a mistake. The benefits my son has experienced are genuine—wider curiosity, more sophisticated questions, greater confidence in exploring unfamiliar terrain. These are real, and they matter.

Tom Wooldridge is the author of the new book End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (Guilford Press, 2026, 140 pages).

Some of what he brings home delights me. He asked recently whether you could power a sailboat by blowing into the sail through a straw. The answer he received was better than the one I would have managed: blowing at your own sail from on board mostly cancels itself out, since you push the air forward and the air pushes you back. Mostly, but not entirely—if the sail catches the stream and turns it around, a little net thrust survives, and if you skip the sail altogether and aim the straw backward, you have built yourself a very small jet engine. He spent the rest of the day on propulsion: rockets, squid, the reason a fan bolted to a sailboat is an old physics puzzle with a surprising answer.

But development is not only about access to knowledge. It is also about the conditions under which a self forms—conditions that include, crucially, the experience of not knowing, of waiting, of struggling toward understanding without guarantee of arrival. These are not inefficiencies to be optimized away. They are the medium through which a mind learns what it is capable of. A child who has never had to sit with a question—who has always had access to a patient, fluent, endlessly available presence to resolve it—may be acquiring knowledge without acquiring the tolerance for uncertainty that makes knowledge genuinely usable.

This is the thing I find myself returning to when I watch my son. He is, in many ways, more intellectually alive than he might otherwise be. He explores further and asks better questions. At the same time, when uncertainty arises, he reaches outward more quickly than he used to—to a presence that is always available, always patient, always responsive. What I cannot yet know is what he is quietly learning to expect: from knowledge, from relationship, and from himself.

We are not conducting a study. We are raising children. And the conditions of childhood have changed again, in ways whose full significance has not yet come into view.

Tom Wooldridge, Psy.D., is a psychoanalyst, founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the roles of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems.

Automation Architect & Lead SDET | Killing flaky tests and breaking pipeline bottlenecks.

Automation Architect & Lead SDET | Killing flaky tests and breaking pipeline bottlenecks.

Automation Architect & Lead SDET | Killing flaky tests and breaking pipeline bottlenecks.

At 11:40 AM on a Monday, nine engineers were sitting in a Slack thread watching a progress bar that had not moved in 45 minutes.

Someone had merged a half-baked Alembic migration into staging-rds-01 and locked the invoices table. Meanwhile, a real 502 bug on /api/v1/exports was actively hitting paying customers in production, and our hotfix could not ship because company policy said every release had to pass a full QA sign-off on staging first.

Four hours later, the hotfix finally went out. Nobody felt safer. Worse, when we checked our incident log that week, we noticed something embarrassing: staging had failed to catch four of our last five production outages anyway.

Why? Because staging had 120 clean seed rows in Postgres, zero concurrent webhook traffic from Stripe, and a Redis instance that never evicted a key. Production had 18 million rows, spiky Monday morning batch jobs, and weird legacy payloads from 2021.

We were paying $2,740 a month in AWS bills to test against a fantasy world.

Two months later, we turned off the shared staging cluster for good.

If your team has more than five developers, a shared staging environment rots in predictable ways:

We still run fast unit tests, contract checks, and ephemeral per-PR Docker Compose smoke tests in GitHub Actions (those cost us about $410/month now). What we killed was the long-lived, shared "pre-production gate" where QA engineers spent half their week babysitting stale seed data.

Instead, we moved real verification into production behind three guardrails: progressive traffic splitting, dark-launch shadow traffic, and isolated synthetic probes.

If you test in production without automatic blast-radius control, you are not doing shift-right testing—you are just breaking things faster.

We replaced our standard Kubernetes Deployment manifests with Argo Rollouts. When a new container image ships, it gets 5% of live traffic for three minutes. An AnalysisTemplate polls Prometheus every 30 seconds. If the 5xx error rate crosses 0.5% or p99 latency jumps above 650ms, Argo aborts the rollout and drains the canary pods in about 45 seconds without a human touching anything.

Here is the exact Rollout and AnalysisTemplate pair we use for our exports-api service:

Notice the two separate pauses: 3 minutes at 5% traffic, then 5 minutes at 25%. Most memory leaks and bad database query plans show up right around the 25% mark when connection pools start filling up.

Canaries are great, but what if you rewrote a pricing calculator or a search query planner and do not want even 5% of real users to see a wrong number?

For read-only and idempotent endpoints, we mirror live production HTTP requests to the new version in the background using Envoy/Nginx traffic shadowing. The user gets the response from the old stable pods. Meanwhile, the canary pod processes the exact same real-world JSON payload, headers, and edge-case query strings—and we compare the status codes and latency in Datadog.

Here is the Nginx Ingress annotation block we used before migrating to Envoy:

Shadow traffic caught a bug in our search query builder that staging never saw in three weeks: real customers were passing 40+ comma-separated filter tags in a single URL, blowing past an internal regex limit and throwing 414 errors.

Shadow traffic tests existing endpoints, and canaries test real user flows. Neither one tests a brand-new multi-step workflow (like onboarding a new workspace or generating a PDF export) before you flip the feature flag on for customers.

That is where our synthetic canary probe comes in.

We created one dedicated internal tenant in production (tenant_id: "canary_synthetic_01"), excluded from all revenue and analytics rollups in Snowflake. Every 60 seconds, a lightweight Kubernetes CronJob runs a Playwright/API probe against production with x-canary-probe: true.

If we are rolling out a new billing flow behind a LaunchDarkly/Unleash feature flag, we turn that flag on only for canary_synthetic_01 first. The probe exercises the real production database, real Redis cluster, and real S3 bucket—then cleans up its own test artifacts at the end of the run.

Here is the TypeScript probe script (scripts/canary-probe.ts) that runs on that 60-second loop:

Two consecutive failures from that CronJob page the on-call engineer and trigger an automatic feature-flag kill-switch via webhook.

Every time I tell someone we killed staging, they assume we just git push --force straight to main and pray.

Not even close. We actually became stricter about pre-merge checks in CI:

What disappeared was the 4-hour human staging queue where nine engineers waited for one brittle cluster to unfreeze.

Moving verification to production is not free. Two mistakes in the first month taught us where the sharp edges are:

Shutting down our shared staging cluster was not magic. The first three weeks were bumpy—we had to train developers to wrap every risky change in a feature flag and add x-canary-probe filtering to our billing reports so synthetic runs didn't inflate customer usage metrics.

Once that settled, though, the numbers spoke for themselves:

If your staging environment costs thousands of dollars a month, blocks releases every Monday, and still lets real bugs slip into production, stop trying to make staging look more like production. It never will. Put your safety nets where the real traffic actually lives. Start with one non-critical service, wire up a 5% Argo canary with a two-metric Prometheus check, and see how fast your team stops missing Monday staging freezes.

We Tested Every REST Endpoint and Missed the Queue That Dropped $62K

#9885. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9883. How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research shows emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper big feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”

Juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

Kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so important for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s important for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”

A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It says “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another big to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

Instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”

The interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the new book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

#9882. The Anchor Effect: Why Destination Footfall Doesn't Equal Retail Demand

- Co-founder, CEO at Ingeocom Ltd, a UK based technology company, - Co-founder, member of the board of directors in Cherry Estates Ltd.

- Co-founder, CEO at Ingeocom Ltd, a UK based technology company, - Co-founder, member of the board of directors in Cherry Estates Ltd.

- Co-founder, CEO at Ingeocom Ltd, a UK based technology company, - Co-founder, member of the board of directors in Cherry Estates Ltd.

On 30 September 2026, Battersea Power Station's developers announced its 50-millionth visitor since the restored landmark opened in October 2022.

The milestone signals destination appeal, not shopfront footfall. It is neither a count of unique customers nor evidence of how visitors move or what they intend to buy.

Here, an anchor is a major district destination, not a conventional shopping-centre tenant. Its benefit depends on visitor routes and spending.

The Wandsworth Council Town Centre Monitoring Report 2025 records vacancy across four completed Battersea zones.

Source: Wandsworth Council, Table 41; survey: 3 October–7 November 2025.

Vacancy ranges from 6% to 38%. Table 41 covers 148 units in completed zones; the report refers to around 150 across the wider development. It records occupancy, not why units were vacant.

The datasets cover different periods (the survey was in autumn 2025; the visitor milestone was announced in September 2026) and establish no link between visits and vacancy. Vacancy may also reflect rents, unit size, lease terms or fit-out.

A destination visitor does not necessarily pass every unit, notice its frontage, enter, or buy. The path to purchase has five stages:

This is a conceptual measurement chain, not a funnel measured at Battersea.

The stages are not interchangeable: destination visits are not frontage footfall, and frontage footfall is not sales. A side-street shop may receive less traffic than one on the main boulevard, even near the same station. Test this with network analysis and observed counts.

These measures answer different spatial questions:

Euclidean buffer - How close is the unit in a straight line?

Network isochrone - How easily can pedestrians reach it?

Frontage flow and visibility - How many people pass the shopfront?

Proximity uses a Euclidean buffer, such as a 300-metre circle. It gives a quick overview but ignores railway lines, buildings and inaccessible entrances.

Accessibility uses a network isochrone: the area reachable within a given time along pedestrian paths. A five-minute isochrone measures reachability, not movement; quiet and busy streets may lie within the same area.

Exposure is pedestrian flow past a frontage and the opportunity to see it. It depends on route choice, entrance position, barriers and sightlines. Network and origin-destination models estimate routes, not actual frontage flow; observed counts or validated mobility data are needed.

Two units may both be 150 metres' walk from a station. Unit A is visible from the main route to nearby offices; Unit B is behind a corner. Their isochrones may match, but A could receive more pass-by exposure. Counts establish the difference.

Footfall has no universal commercial value: its importance depends on the tenant's business model, opening hours and customer behavior.

Estimated Revenue = Catchment Footfall × Frontage Capture Rate × Store Entry Rate × Purchase Conversion × Average Transaction Value

The variables represent catchment volume, frontage capture, entry, purchase conversion and average spend. Use a consistent period; if footfall is counted at the shopfront, omit the first two stages. This estimates sales, not profit.

OCR = Occupancy Costs/Store Revenue × 100%

The Occupancy Cost Ratio compares revenue with rent and defined property charges, such as service charges. Use consistent cost definitions and revenue excluding VAT.

High exposure does not guarantee viability. If occupancy costs exceed what achievable revenue can support, the tenant may struggle. OCR is not profitability-gross margin, staffing and other expenses still matter-but it links location quality to the cost of securing it.

Different retail formats, different flow profiles

An anchor can generate complementary demand or retain spending in its own restaurants, cafés and shops. The effect depends on tenant category, routes and overlap between offers.

Move from broad context to unit-level evidence:

A single footfall score cannot capture the commercial case. Identify the assumptions driving the result and the evidence supporting them.

Developer metrics show destination activity, not movement between zones, repeat visits, or traffic at a particular unit. Check the counting methodology before treating a milestone as a unique-visitor figure.

Municipal reports, such as Wandsworth Council's survey, provide occupancy and commercial-use information, not reasons for vacancy, store sales, conversion rates or lease terms.

Transport datasets from TfL Open Data and its API portal help establish accessibility. Station-level passenger data does not measure pedestrian movement along individual streets or shopfronts.

For an individual Battersea unit, these sources cannot show which routes carry the most pedestrians or count shopfront passers-by. That requires geocoded entrances, route analysis and observed or validated flow data. Accessibility maps are not footfall maps.

Battersea's visitor milestone and Wandsworth Council's survey describe different aspects of the development: destination activity and vacancy across completed zones. Neither explains an individual unit's performance.

Proximity, accessibility and exposure must be kept separate. A unit can be close to an attraction but poorly positioned on pedestrian routes, easy to reach but receive little spontaneous traffic, or busy yet fail to attract customers suited to the tenant's offer.

Connect spatial evidence to observed movement and store economics: estimate frontage flow, model sales conversion and test whether revenue supports occupancy costs. That is the difference between measuring destination activity and assessing a retail location.

Hybrid Work Broke the Ground Floor: Why Office Headcount No Longer Predicts Retail Demand
