#9816. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9814. 12 Powdered Gravy Mixes, Ranked Worst To Best

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

As most pro home chefs will tell you, making gravy from scratch isn't exactly rocket science. With the help of a little flour, butter, and broth, you could be on your way to a delicious gravy in just a few minutes. Still, there may be times when you simply aren't feeling up to it — whether you've had a rough week or are drowning in to-dos, packets of powdered gravy mix can prove a simple, flavorful fix.

Even so, the kind of store-bought gravy mix you choose matters — after all, anything you're planning to drown your meat and taters in had better be good. That's why I decided to make it my mission to test some of the most popular powdered gravy options in my area in hopes of offering my honest opinion about which truly deserves a spot in your kitchen

In the upcoming post, I'm giving a complete rundown of every store-bought powdered gravy mix I could find, including the pricing, size, and taste of each. Bear in mind that the details mentioned in this article are subject to change and that the gravy packet selection featured here may not be reflective of what's available in your area. With that, join me as I prepare, taste, and rank 12 store-bought powdered gravy mixes from worst to best.

Prices are as of the date of publication and may vary based on region.

Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix is a no-frills Walmart-branded product that is, surprisingly, one of the costlier options on the list when you consider its price per unit. Though tagged at only 92 cents per packet, each pack contains .87 ounces, meaning you'll pay roughly $1.06 per ounce of powdered gravy.

Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix is prepared using the standard 1 cup of water per 1 packet of mix, and its ingredients include monosodium glutamate (otherwise known as "MSG"), which may pose a problem for gravy lovers who may be sensitive to the ingredient. I tore open the packet, and its unappetizing, artificial smell hit me right away. Once cooked, the mixture turned creamy and thick, but its color seemed unnatural, especially when compared to homemade. I gave it a hesitant taste, and nope, not good — Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix tasted like stale chicken and literally made me gag.

Would I recommend purchasing Great Value Chicken Gravy Mix? No way. Not only does its bright yellow color not resemble any chicken gravy I've ever made, but the taste was barely tolerable. I'm sure you could try improving this store-bought gravy with Worcestershire sauce, but I say, if it's convenience you seek, there are other options more deserving of your coin than this one.

I hate to have to rank yet another Great Value powdered gravy mix so close to the bottom of the list, but it simply cannot be helped. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix is a bit cheaper than its chicken-flavored counterpart — expect to pay 78 cents per .87 ounces, which works out to around 89.7 cents per ounce of powdered gravy. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix doesn't contain the MSG that the chicken flavor includes, but that doesn't mean I recommend purchasing it — like the former, it has a weird smell and taste that I simply can't get past.

I prepared Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix according to the package directions and watched it bubble and simmer on the stove. The mix eventually turned the typical light brown color normally associated with turkey gravy and had an uber-thick consistency. I let it cool slightly before giving it a quick taste — sadly, it had the same stomach-churning qualities as the previous flavor. Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix tasted woefully artificial; in fact, the additives or chemicals present in the gravy were just about the only thing I could taste. Needless to say, I would never dish up Great Value Turkey Gravy Mix to guests at Thanksgiving — you'd be better off leaving not-so-Great Value picks like this one on the shelf.

Before offering my opinion here, I have to be honest and say I'm not a person who prepares peppered gravy often. That said, I'm willing to bet Southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix doesn't quite encapsulate its classic flavor the way other options do.

Southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix costs $1.22 per 2.75 ounces, with a unit price of 44.4 cents per ounce. As is typical for many peppered gravy mixes on the market, this packet contains a little more powdered gravy mix per pack than other varieties and flavors. Its preparation requires more water, too — you'll need 1 ¾ cups this time around versus the usual 1 cup.

Southeastern Mills Peppered Gravy Mix tasted annoyingly bland, with a flavor very similar to what you'd get if you added black pepper to plain cream. Though thick, it had no richness of flavor, and I couldn't imagine it doing much to elevate anyone's sausage gravy. I flipped the packet over and was surprised by what I saw on the ingredient list: Palm oil and modified food starch were the first ingredients mentioned, which is hardly a good way to start a high-quality gravy, if you ask me. As I said, I am by no means an expert in peppered gravy, but based on first impressions alone, I'd say skip this brand and opt for other, richer, more flavorful brands on the market.

If you're surprised to see McCormick Brown Gravy Mix ranked lower on the list, join the club. I, for one, adore brown gravy, and with McCormick being one of the most popular gravy and seasoning brands on the market, I figured I'd be in for a real treat. Expect to pay 97 cents for .87 ounces of it, making each ounce cost roughly $1.12.

When cooking up McCormick Brown Gravy Mix, I couldn't help but feel excited — its texture was thick and glossy, and the gravy had a deep brown hue that just screamed umami beef. It even had the savory, enticing aroma of a succulent pot roast, so imagine my surprise when I discovered the gravy tastes, quite literally, like nothing.

That's right — McCormick Brown Gravy Mix features a flavor so weak I could barely taste anything at all. To think McCormick Brown Gravy Mix smelled and looked so great without delivering flavor even half of what was teased is mind-boggling. Needless to say, McCormick Brown Gravy Mix isn't worth the buy — I'd recommend picking up some beef broth and making your own simple brown gravy or choosing one of the higher-ranking varieties over this one.

Though not the best out there, Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix is a dark horse in terms of taste and performance. The gravy comes sold in an .87-ounce pack and was priced at 83 cents, about 95 cents per ounce. It contains artificial ingredients along with a host of additives, but hey, if that kinda stuff doesn't bother you, feel free to ignore those stats.

I went into my tasting of Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix with low expectations — almost every Amazon Grocery item I've sampled in the past left me underwhelmed. Much to my amazement, Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix held its own in terms of consistency and aroma — it was a bit thinner than a few other options on the list, yes, but still managed to be just thick enough. I also found its glossy deep brown appearance mesmerizing, and its smell rich and meaty, just the way a good brown gravy should be.

Going in for a slurp, I didn't walk away disappointed — though the flavor was nowhere near as potent as its aroma, it was leaps and bounds better than McCormick. I could clearly taste its beefy notes, and its umami depth was decent overall. One thing I will say is that Amazon Grocery Brown Gravy Mix tastes slightly watered down; still, I think it will get you by if you're looking for a tasty, inexpensive brown gravy to crown your mashers.

Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix is pretty good; though not a peppered gravy kinda gal, I have an appreciation for this brand and would recommend it over Southeastern Mills any day. This mix comes in a 2.75-ounce packet, only this time, you'll need to add 2 cups of water instead of the 1 ¾ cups Southeastern Mills requires. Each packet costs $1.33, meaning you'll cop this powdered peppered gravy for about 48.4 cents per ounce.

When cooking up Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix, the first thing I noticed was its golden hue. The yellowish tinge of the Pioneer-branded gravy made it more attractive than the stark white presentation of Southeastern Mills. It was just as thick as the former brand, if not thicker, though whether or not its flavor would prove better was yet to be seen.

So, how'd Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix taste? Though I still consider its flavor mundane compared to traditional chicken or brown gravies, Pioneer Peppered Gravy Mix had more depth than Southeastern Mills. It's not listed in the ingredients, but there seemed to be a hint of butter flavor in the mixture — this deepened the taste and added complexity. All in all, if I were to grab a packet of peppered gravy for breakfast, this is the brand I'd get — not only does it look better, but its taste is pretty decent, too.

McCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix wasn't too bad — it isn't something I'd choose over homemade gravy for Thanksgiving dinner, but it's good if you're in a pinch and want something cheap. The gravy comes sold in a .87-ounce packet for $1.63, and while this might not sound super expensive, it's actually a little pricier than others, at $1.87 per ounce.

McCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix yields a light brown color I found fitting for turkey gravy — it certainly looked the part, featuring a medium-thick consistency and glossy appearance. McCormick Turkey Gravy Seasoning Mix has a poultry-like flavor that's pleasing but leans more chicken than turkey in my opinion. Nevertheless, I consider this turkey gravy option to be one of the punchier, more robust picks out there, and though I don't necessarily consider it holiday worthy, it might be good to have a packet or two in your pantry for days when you're low on time.

Fire & Smoke Society Big Sunday Brown Gravy Mix is a super unique option, and though I probably wouldn't buy it again, you might consider trying it if you're looking to sample something outside of the norm. The packaging here has the kind of aesthetic that makes you think it's fancy by looks alone — its price also stands out, at $1.72 per 1-ounce pack, working out to $1.72 per ounce. A quick scan of the ingredients reveals several surprises — though not a clean ingredient pick by any means, some additions — like cumin, chili powder, and even coffee — left me curious as to what kind of flavor I was in for.

I prepared the gravy as per its 1 cup to 1 packet instructions and immediately noticed a difference in its texture compared to the others. Fire & Smoke Society Big Sunday Brown Gravy Mix yields a thinner, silkier texture than most. Its aroma was totally unexpected, as it was more akin to grill spices than savory beef. After tasting Fire & Smoke Society's Big Sunday Brown Gravy Mix, I found myself torn — the taste wasn't gross, but didn't encompass the type of flavor I expect from a classic brown gravy.

Is Fire & Smoke Society Big Sunday Brown Gravy Mix good? Yes! Would I buy it again? Probably not. Blame it on my traditional taste buds, but for me, this powdered gravy mix is just OK.

Is there a difference between country and peppered gravy? Apparently, there is, and as it stands, I prefer the former. Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was a breath of fresh air flavor-wise, but I suppose that isn't surprising given I love practically anything that the Kinder brand produces. Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was priced at $1.72 per 1.9 ounces at my local Walmart, working out to about 90.5 cents per ounce.

Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning was truly phenomenal in terms of taste and texture. First and foremost, the gravy recommends preparing it with 2 cups of milk, which automatically gave it a richer, sweeter finish. Once cooked, the gravy was thick and featured a stark white appearance flecked with tons of contrasting black pepper throughout.

Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning tastes almost identical to creamy, buttery, garlicky mashed potatoes, no spuds needed. I'd imagine this would taste incredible paired with creamy taters, and I wouldn't hesitate to dish it up as a turkey topper during the holidays. As if things couldn't get better, Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning uses fairly clean ingredients, with nowhere near as much of the ick featured in other powdered gravy mixes on the list. With all things considered, Kinder's Classic Country Gravy Dry Seasoning is one of my favorite powdered gravy mixes on the market.

Simply Organic Roasted Chicken Gravy Seasoning Mix costs $1.72 for .85 ounces making it one of the most expensive powdered gravy mixes on the market at $2.02 per ounce. It's the only gluten-free organic chicken option on the list, and I honestly didn't expect it to taste as good as it did. Not that I have anything against organic foods — I actually love them and find the use of minimal ingredients refreshing. Still, in the world of gravy, I guess I just didn't expect a natural option like this one to hold its own when pitted against others containing various flavor-boosting additives. Thankfully, this humble pick from Simply Organic proved me wrong.

Simply Organic chicken gravy calls for the standard 1 cup of gravy packet seasoning per 1 cup of water. As it cooked, it began to take on a sauce-like consistency that was thick, glossy, and light brown. I gave it a taste and was floored — this organic pick boasted a flavor way better than any other store-bought chicken gravy I've tried.

Simply Organic chicken gravy had a bold, savory, and garlicky flavor beautifully enhanced with prominent notes of celery seed. Thus, though expensive, you can rest assured that your money is going to good use — Simply Organic Roasted Chicken Gravy Seasoning Mix is a phenomenal replacement for homemade when you don't feel like whipping up chicken gravy on your own.

Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix is the only organic brown gravy on the list, and let me tell you, it did not disappoint. Unlike its chicken-flavored predecessor, Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix is slightly cheaper, at 1 ounce for $1.72 ( $1.72 per ounce). Being the organic grab that it is, expect Simply Organic brown gravy to be non-GMO and free of artificial colors, flavors, and ingredients. One of its best attributes is its use of cornstarch rather than flour, as this makes it a great option for people looking to ditch wheat.

I was delighted to find Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix packing so much flavor — after the previous brown gravy duds, I didn't have much hope that there was a truly good packaged option out there. In truth, Simply Organic's brown gravy is one of the most flavorful in its class — it was one of the few to truly capture the beefy, oniony savor I come to expect from a good homemade brown gravy.

One thing to note is that Simply Organic brown gravy has a medium consistency and a color a lot lighter than others in its category. Still, Simply Organic Brown Gravy Seasoning Mix would make the perfect companion to roast beef or over creamy mashed potatoes, and I doubt anyone would be able to detect the difference between it and homemade.

Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy is unlike any other gravy I've tried — I had never sampled jalapeño gravy before, nor did I know it existed. Now that it's on my radar, in my cabinet it will stay. It's really that good, even if it is $2.50 per 2.82-ounce packet (89 cents per ounce)!

Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy contains no artificial flavors, which to me is pretty impressive. Though not gluten-free like the aforementioned Simply Organic picks, it does at least contain fewer additives while still managing to achieve unbelievably thick results. You only need to use 2 cups of water per packet to cash in on this irresistibly luscious golden gravy; its texture was so rich and smooth my mouth watered just at the sight of it.

Aside from its tantalizing consistency, Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy tastes incredible — I'd describe its flavor as similar to high-quality jalapeño nacho cheese, but with less emphasis on the cheese. It's quite spicy, and though not unbearably so, still isn't something I'd recommend offering to kids. All in all, Yellowstone Jalapeño Gravy is an amazing option I'd buy over and over again — try it on fried chicken cutlets, potatoes, stuffing, or hot sandwiches. Yum!

The 12 powdered gravy mixes selected for this article were chosen based on availability in my area, with most sourced from Walmart and Amazon. Each gravy mix was ranked primarily based on texture and flavor, although other factors, like ingredients and pricing, were considered. As always, pricing and availability are subject to change.

#9812. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

Cover photo by Patrick Marinello; food styling by Yekaterina Boytsova.

Justine Lee is a food writer, recipe developer, and culinary consultant based in New York City. In her free time, she is actively on a hunt for a good almond croissant.

#9810. 12 Costco Cakes You Should Be Picking Up In November 2026

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

From birthdays to holiday gatherings, a beautiful cake can be the star attraction and make an ordinary occasion feel extraordinary. Thanksgiving is right around the corner, and while pies are often the go-to dessert for this holiday, serving your guests something unexpected in the form of a cake can turn your dinner into a memorable feast, especially if they have multiple meals to attend. Sure, you can make one from scratch, but with all the activity and planning surrounding this holiday, you may just want to opt for something store-bought, and Costco offers the perfect solution.

The Costco bakery offers a huge range, from decadent layer cakes in crowd-pleasing flavors to rich cheesecakes — which aren't technically cakes, though we're including them here anyway. There are also some Italian-style specialties, a truly seasonal option, and one flourless chocolate cake that will bring a touch of luxury to your table.

Keep in mind that the wholesale club requires a membership for customers to shop there. If you're not already a member, this list of cakes may convince you to join. Just remember that prices and availability may vary by location and that some cakes may only be available to order online.

When it comes to Thanksgiving, few people would argue with the idea that the holiday isn't complete without at least one pumpkin dessert. However, instead of serving the expected pie this year, opt for this cheesecake — in addition to a creamy base full of intense pumpkin flavor, the whole dessert is topped with pecans and a generous drizzle of caramel sauce.

A two-pack of Ferrara's Bakery 8-inch Pumpkin Cheesecake with Caramel and Pecan Topping is available at Costco for $119.99.

Panettone is an Italian delicacy made from a yeasted dough studded with dried and candied fruit, and it has a lightly sweet flavor and fluffy texture. This bready cake is incredibly versatile and can be the foundation for many fall recipes. Try tearing it into pieces to make a delicious bread pudding, or follow Giada De Laurentiis's suggestion for leftover panettone and use it to top a holiday salad.

Chiostro di Saronno Panettone Classico is available at Costco for $29.99.

Whether you're starting your day with a cup of joe, pausing for a midafternoon pick-me-up, or finishing a meal with coffee or tea, this cake from Collin Street Bakery should be on the table. It comes in a beautiful white tin and includes a cup of icing for drizzling, while the warming cinnamon spice feels like a hug on your palate. It also makes a beautiful gift.

Collin Street Bakery Cinnamon Coffee Cake is available at Costco for $34.99.

Collin Street Bakery is a Texas-based company, and the Lone Star State is known for producing pecans, so you're almost guaranteed to have delicious pecan flavor in this pair of cakes. Besides containing the rich nuts, each one is chock-full of either pineapple or glacéed apricots. The batter for these cakes is also sweetened with honey.

Collin Street Bakery Apricot & Pineapple Pecan Cake Bundle is available at Costco for $64.99.

For some, Christmas cannot arrive soon enough. Fortunately, Costco has a little preview of the holiday for these individuals in the form of this mini pecan cake bundle, which includes four favorite flavors: cherry fudge cake, pineapple cake, blonde cake, and a classic fruitcake. If you're wondering how fruitcakes can last all year, adding a heavy dose of alcohol can help preserve them.

The Collin Street Bakery Mini Pecan Cake Bundle is available at Costco for $49.99.

The Knipschildt brand once held the Guinness World Record for the most expensive chocolate truffle in the world, but you don't need to take out a loan to enjoy this dessert. This flourless cake features a layer of rich chocolate ganache and is finished with the chocolatier's signature truffles. It's a striking cake that will bring a bit of sophistication to your next gathering.

Knipschildt Chocopologie Truffle Flourless Chocolate Cake is available at Costco for $69.99.

Tiramisu may seem like tres leches, but it's an entirely different dessert. Its name translates to "lift me up," and while traditional versions may come in a square format, this one from Ferrara's Bakery is round and features an attractive collar of brown and white stripes. The bakery makes its own ladyfingers and douses them in coffee and coffee liqueur before layering them with sweetened mascarpone cheese.

A two-pack of Ferrara's Bakery 8-inch Tiramisu Cake is available at Costco for $99.99.

If you love the combination of chocolate and peanut butter, then this cake is for you. The base is made from a fudge brownie, and it's topped with layers of peanut butter mousse and decadent chocolate cake. As if that's not enough, the whole confection gets a crown of brownie pieces, chocolate fudge, and peanut butter chips.

For the consummate chocolate lover, no other flavors should get in the way of a chocolate cake, and this one is nothing short of perfection. It starts with four layers of rich chocolate sponge sandwiching velvety milk chocolate mousse; then, the entire thing gets covered in chocolate ganache and a coating of chocolate shavings that resemble bark, making this cake look like an edible tree trunk. It's pre-sliced, too, ensuring that everyone gets a fair share.

Try drizzling it with dulce de leche and finishing it with chopped walnuts, or top it with apple pie filling and a sprinkling of mixed spices for an autumnal take on a classic. This carrot cake features thick layers of cake and cream cheese frosting and is covered with a generous coating of vanilla buttercream. For an elegant touch, it's topped with silk cherry blossoms, and comes in a striking box tied with a beautiful ribbon, too. If you're not a fan of nuts or raisins, this cake is free of both, so nothing gets in the way of the spiced carrot flavor.

The Cake Bake Shop 8-inch Round Carrot Cake is available at Costco for $159.99.

#9807. 19 non-traditional Thanksgiving desserts that aren't pie : Cakes, cookies, and even a tiramisu for your holiday dessert table.

Yes, Thanksgiving is a pie-centric holiday. But what if you don’t like pie? Or maybe you just don’t want it. Either way, we’ve got lots of non-pie Thanksgiving desserts, from spiced pumpkin cupcakes to sugary apple cobblers, plus plenty of autumnal cakes.

This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Bundt Pan Set

This dessert demonstrates how to dress up a crumb cake for fall: Top velvety sour cream cake with a juicy layer of apples, then crown the cake with a generous layer of apple pie-spiced streusel.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Clearjel

Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

Get the recipe: Sweet Potato Sheet Cake with Marshmallow Frosting (make it gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Soft Swirl Bundt Pan

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

“Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

Don’t be fooled by its stodgy name or humble appearance: This cake is so good, we named it our #1 best fall recipe! In fact, my colleague Jessica Battilana made it for Thanksgiving last year and declared it the biggest hit of the day; her guests fell in love with the moist, apple-loaded cake and fudgy brown sugar frosting.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

If your biggest complaint about PSLs is that there's not enough coffee flavor, look to this Bundt cake, which has an espresso powder swirl running through the tender pumpkin crumb and a coffee glaze to finish the whole thing off.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Golden Wheat Flour

If you don’t want to fuss with pie, we suggest making a cobbler instead. This fruit-filled version pairs juicy spiced apples with a crackly brown sugar crust — both prep and serving are easy, and the resulting cobbler will absolutely steal the show.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Apples are great, but seasonal pears deserve some love too. This simple cake, made with a combination of almond and all-purpose flours, has a rich, buttery texture and an almost marzipan-like chew. Studded with fragrant cubes of ripe pear, it's an elegant after-dinner dessert.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Almond Flour

The boozy Bundt cake features potent maple flavor thanks to the 1/2 cup (!) of maple syrup in the batter, plus the sticky maple-and-rum glaze to finish. Made with cake flour and sour cream, the cake itself is dense and velvety, like all great pound cakes should be.

Get the recipe: Maple Pound Cake with Maple-Rum Glaze

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

Instead of slicing and serving dessert, bake every guest their own individual mini cake. Start with a moist, spicy sheet cake, then use a biscuit cutter or overturned glass to cut rounds for individual layer cakes sandwiched with cream cheese frosting.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Apple Pie Spice

Rich, silky, and balanced, this cheesecake is the kind of dessert that wins people (even cheesecake skeptics) over at first bite. Pecans are blended into the crust to add a subtle nutty flavor and delicate crunch. The ultra-creamy filling gets its sweetness from brown sugar and maple syrup, while heavy cream gives it an especially luxurious texture.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Maple Syrup

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

For a little French flair at your Thanksgiving table, make this classic tarte tatin. This dessert can be a little fussy, but we’ve endlessly tested our version to make sure it goes off without a hitch in your kitchen. And it’s worth it for the deeply caramelized apples layered over shattering pastry.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” round cake pan

Tiramisu gets a fall-forward spin in this coffeeshop-inspired dessert. Just like a caramel macchiato combines espresso, steamed milk, and a generous caramel drizzle, this twist on classic tiramisu layers salted caramel sauce between espresso-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone filling.

Get the recipe: Caramel Macchiato Tiramisu

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Espresso Powder

Make serving Thanksgiving dessert a breeze by baking up a big batch of cupcakes. These are packed with pumpkin flavor and spice, then finished with an easy swoop of cream cheese frosting. If you really want to level up your presentation, check out these cupcake decorating techniques for a pro-level finish.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cupcakes (make them gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Unbleached Cake Flour

This holiday-ready version of our five-star Everyday Olive Oil Cake is adorned with a big red bow in the form of a simple but stunning cranberry glaze. Made by cooking cranberries with orange juice, then whisking the mixture with confectioners’ sugar, the icing adds a bright tartness that complements the rich cake.

Get the recipe: Cranberry-Orange Olive Oil Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: King Arthur Square Pan

#9806. The Egg McMuffin Order You Can Only Find In Canada

McDonald's breakfast is a thing of beauty, and if you think we've got it good here in the States, you probably haven't seen what's sitting on Canada's breakfast menu. Alongside familiar faves, you'll find items Americans can't order, the most envy-inducing among them arguably being the Egg BLT McMuffin. Once you hear what's in it, don't be surprised if you catch yourself planning a trip to our northern neighbor.

The Egg BLT starts with McDonald's signature ring-shaped steamed (not fried) egg, paired with hickory-smoked bacon, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomato, then finished with a creamy, mayo-like sauce and a slice of cheese, all stacked on a toasted English muffin. A second version uses nearly identical ingredients but swaps the whole leaves for shredded lettuce. You can only get this variation at McDonald's restaurants located inside Walmart stores — part of a decades-old partnership that once placed roughly 1,000 outposts in the retail chain. McDonald's later closed hundreds of them as drive-thrus became the main source of sales, though Walmart continues to host many locations in Canada.

To get your hands on an Egg BLT McMuffin in the U.S., you'll have to get creative. Your best bet is to start with a Bacon, Egg & Cheese McMuffin, which already ticks off half the ingredients. Ask for a touch of mayo, which gets you close to the sauce of the Canadian original. Since lettuce and tomatoes are lunchtime items, your odds improve near the end of breakfast hours when stores are prepping the lunch menu — you'll likely have to order them at the counter or window.

The Egg BLT might have already convinced you to add McDonald's to your itinerary next time you're in Canada, but it's not the only breakfast item worth the detour. One that caught our eye was the Mighty McGriddles. While the U.S. offers the Bacon, Egg & Cheese and Sausage, Egg & Cheese varieties separately, the Canadian version puts both to shame by stacking a double helping of hickory-smoked bacon, a sausage patty, egg, and cheese between two maple-flavored griddle cakes — a gloriously overstuffed creation that lives up to its name. The Mighty McMuffin follows the same logic, coming loaded with both meats for anyone who can never decide between the two.

Another familiar face on Canadian McDonald's breakfast menus is the bagel, though while America only offers plain, Canada also serves sesame and everything varieties. You can even order one toasted with butter or Philadelphia cream cheese — widely known as the best store-bought brand — as if you're at a proper bagel shop.

Canada's McDonald's restaurants aren't afraid to put a twist on U.S. staples, and they also introduce new items altogether. You won't find chicken anywhere on the standard U.S. breakfast menu, which makes the Chicken McGriddles feel like a curveball up north. The simple yet delicious sandwich pairs a breaded chicken patty with two sweet, maple-flavored griddle cakes for some serious sweet-and-savory fusion.

#9804. 14 French Desserts You Should Try Once In Your Life

French cuisine is largely known for its decadent textures, flavors, and presentations, and this includes a long list of regional desserts. We all know about croissants, and, yes, when infused with the right sweet elements, they definitely count as a dessert, but that's just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to French desserts. In fact, there is a seemingly never-ending list of eye-catching sweet treats that hail from the country. The ones found below, though, are so mouthwateringly delicious that everyone should try them at least once in their lives.

If you aren't already familiar with French desserts, it doesn't matter if you are fluent in the language or not; the names of the country's culinary creations don't always alert you to what they actually are. With this in mind, if you're interested in sampling a few — why wouldn't you be? — but aren't sure where to start, we can help point you in the right direction. So, get your fork and spoon ready, because once you learn about the collection of French desserts below, you'll be dying to get your hands on them.

The tart Tatin may have a fancy name, but don't let that fool you. It is actually akin to an apple pie, just flipped upside down — and there's nothing extravagant about that. The French version of the dessert also has humble origins. As the story goes, in the late 1800s, Caroline (of Caroline and Stephanie Tatin's Inn, located south of Paris) forgot to put a crust on the bottom of her apple pie. Due to being exceptionally busy, she decided to put it on top instead and see what would happen. When she took it out of the oven and flipped it over, she saw that her misstep led to a happy result: The apples were beautifully caramelized. When she served it to the inn's guests, it was an immediate success, and the tarte Tatin was officially born.

Creating a tart Tatin is fairly accessible to novice home cooks. It only calls for five ingredients: apples, flour, butter, eggs, and sugar. The trickiest part is arranging the slices of fruit in a decorative way on the bottom of the pan. Actually, despite her massive culinary repertoire, Ina Garten admits it is the recipe she makes most because it is not only delicious, but easy to create, as well. If it's good enough for Garten to come back time and time again, you'd better believe it's a French dessert everyone should give a go at least once.

Crème brûlée is one of the most easily recognizable and widely popular French desserts in the United States, but, interestingly enough, its origins are somewhat disputed. France, England, and Spain all claim to be the birthplace of the dessert. Regardless, since its invention, wherever that happened to be, there's no doubt it has fully integrated itself into traditional French cuisine, and if you've never had the joy of eating one before, you are truly missing out.

In its most basic format, crème brûlée is made with just four ingredients: egg yolks, sugar, heavy cream, and vanilla bean. While simple, the elements come together to form a creamy, custardy delight. Then, the top is scorched to form a layer of burnt sugar that's to die for. Topping it with a couple of fresh berries is also customary, but either way, it is simplicity at its finest. In fact, this is one case where the sum is much greater than its parts. In addition to the sweet, rich flavor of the custard itself, part of the fun of eating one is using a spoon to crack the burnt layer on top. It not only adds a caramelized taste but contributes textural variation, and that is always a plus. Whether you decide to try your hand at making crème brûlée yourself or choose to seek it out from a restaurant, it's a French dessert that's worth your attention.

Éclairs have been around since the 1860s, and today, they are one of the more popular French desserts found in the United States. For good reason, too; they are tasty enough to go down in a flash. Speaking of which, the word directly translates to lightning.

Name and popularity aside, éclairs are made with choux pastry, which is similar to doughnut pastry, but devoid of baking soda, baking powder, and yeast, and relies on steam to rise. As a result, after being formed into long cylindrical pieces, the dough cooks up to be exceptionally light and airy. That's just the start of the legendary éclair, though. They are also filled with pastry cream or custard and then topped with either fondant or ganache icing — both of which are harder styles of icing, so you can still feel free to enjoy éclairs with your hands.

Arguably, the most popular flavor of éclair is chocolate, but thanks to the versatility of the choux pastry shell, they are welcoming to a world of other flavors as well. Everything from caramel to pistachio to Nutella to strawberry to matcha with chocolate and beyond can be found enhancing the delightful little pastry.

French yogurt cake, or gâteaux au yaourt in the native language, is another easy yet extremely satisfying dessert that deserves some time in the spotlight. In France, it is a popular recipe for kids to learn, likely because of the simple recipe, which calls for three eggs, one part oil, one part yogurt, two parts sugar, three parts flour, and leavening. Even so, when it comes out of the oven, you have a drool-worthy, slightly tangy cake that is moister than pound cake (if you can fathom that) while still presenting a delicate crumb.

Since French yogurt cake is not a common restaurant offering, if you want to give it a taste, you'll likely have to make one yourself. Or, at the very least, enlist a friend to do it — um, mom? Thankfully, though, it is one of the more straightforward must-try French desserts out there, so it should be attainable for even the most novice home cooks. The simplicity of the French yogurt cake also makes it prime for a plethora of flavor infusions. So, if you want to add citrus, or brandy, or fruit to the mix, go right ahead.

Crêpes are a delicately thin pancake-like creation that's ready and waiting for a world of flavor and ingredient infusions. Still, a Crêpes Suzette is quite possibly the most delicious and famous version of them all. It consists of classic crêpes in a sauce made of sugar, orange juice, and an orange liqueur, like Gran Marnier. The entire thing is also smothered in brandy and set on fire, which leads to a caramelized, citrusy, sweet flambé sauce that will draw just about anyone in. Heck, even watching a chef prepare one catches the eye, and that's why it's often done in full view when ordered in a restaurant.

Interestingly enough, crêpes Suzette is another iconic French dessert that was first created by accident — and this particular story is not disputed. In 1895, Henri Carpentier, a 14-year-old assistant waiter at the Maitre at Monte Carlo's Cafe Paris, was preparing dessert for the Prince of Wales (who'd later become King Edward VII of England). While doing so, he accidentally caught the cordials he was working with on fire, and instead of becoming flustered and starting over from scratch, he tasted the sauce and realized he'd come up with something extraordinary.

Don't let the flambé scare you too much if you want to try creating one at home; it truly does lead to exceptional flavor. However, you can still make a tasty rendition sans the potential fire hazard; it just won't be quite as authentic.

First and foremost, Mont Blanc is known for being the highest mountain in the Alps. However, for those in the know, it is also a delectable French sweet treat with Alpine-inspired appeal. In fact, when created, the Mont Blanc dessert resembles a snow-capped mountain peak, so the name is more than fitting. The exact origins of it is uncertain, but a reigning theory is that it was developed in Paris, France, in the 19th century. During that era, chestnuts started to grow in popularity in the region, and people began incorporating them into sweet dishes, instead of the customary savory ones.

The main components of a Mont Blanc dessert are as follows: It starts with a crisp meringue base, which is topped with thin strands of chestnut purée, and then finished off with a pile of whipped cream. Traditionally, a vermicelli tip is used to pipe the chestnut puree, but other shapes are also common. Either way, though, the yummy chestnut puree is the star of the show, offering a nutty, rich flavor that offsets the creamy whipped cream and meringue in a delightful way.

Hailing from the Basque region in southwest France, the Gâteau Basque became widely popular in the 19th century. Its growth in the culinary scene is largely attributed to a particular baker, Marianne Hirigoyen, who first sold them in local markets before opening a brick-and-mortar bakery. Since then, the gâteau Basque's acceptance into French culinary tradition has been more than cemented. Actually, fast-forward to today, and there's now a museum and a two-day festival in October dedicated to the dessert. If that doesn't tell you exactly why it is a must-try French recipe, we don't know what would.

Whether you call them canelé, cannelé de Bordeaux, or canelé Bordelais, these yummy little French pastries are time-consuming to make — the dough needs to rest for up to 24 hours before baking. Even so, their delectable mix of textures and delicious buttery, custard-y flavors are worth the effort used to make them and then some.

Small and cylindrical with fluted edges, the center of canelés are made with flour, milk, sugar, butter, vanilla bean, eggs, salt, and rum. Once mixed with care, the dough rests for an extended time before baking in copper molds. After they're cooked, a delicious coating of edible beeswax and butter fills the molds and is also poured over the top before baking again. When that's done, you're left with delicious bite-sized (well, almost) custard-filled cakes featuring a caramelized crust on the exterior. Considering miniature copper fluted molds are not a customary tool in most homes, canelés aren't the first dessert we recommend trying to make at home. However, if you ever see them in a French bakery or restaurant, you'd be a fool not to give them a try.

Opera cake is one of the coffee desserts that are always worth ordering, and guess what? It's also a French dessert everyone should try at least once. That is, of course, if you know what's good for you — and in this case, we truly hope you do.

Created by Cyrique Gavillon, the opera cake is just as much a thing of beauty as it is a delectable flavor wonderland. A rectangular-shaped cake at heart, it is made with alternating layers of coffee syrup-soaked almond cake, buttercream, and ganache, and then topped with a rich dark chocolate icing. Once completed, it not only looks stunning, but provides your palate with a mix of nutty, chocolatey, creamy, rich, coffee flavors that are hard to beat. Yes, it sounds a whole lot like tiramisu when the elements are taken at face value, but it is a delightful dessert all its own when it comes to how the ingredients come together. Plus, it's French, not Italian. Just saying.

While simple to make, the Île flottante presents itself as an elegant dish, and as such, is a mainstay in French cuisine. In fact, while it's said French people prefer to purchase dessert from a local bakery, it is one recipe many natives still have in their repertoire. It just so happened to be Julia Child's favorite old-school dessert, as well. Since she is credited with bringing French cuisine to the United States and helping it grow in popularity, following her lead regarding the greatest culinary hits of the country just makes sense.

Similar to éclairs, which we've already discussed, profiteroles are made with hollowed-out choux pastry, filled with custard or cream, and topped with icing. What sets them apart is their shape. Instead of being long and cylindrical, profiteroles are formed into small bite-sized balls. As a result, they are the perfect sweet treat for bringing to a gathering or munching on if you simply want a few bites. However, once you get a taste of their scrumptious textures and flavors, trying to eat just one will be quite a complicated task.

Again, like éclairs, the most common icing flavor for profiteroles is chocolate. Still, they come in a myriad of other flavors, as well, so they have what it takes to pique the interest of many. For example, if chocolate is too one-dimensional for you — we are judging you — you can also make chocolate hazelnut profiteroles, vanilla ones, or just about any other flavor you can dream up.

Last but certainly not least on our list of French desserts you need to try is clafoutis. The name may sound posh, but it's actually another sweet treat that's incredibly easy to make, so you don't have to be an established French baker to create one at home. Plus, it may be a dessert, but it is also acceptable to eat it for breakfast. Okay, now we are really listening.

Clafoutis consists of fruit smothered with a thick custard made from sugar, flour, milk, and eggs. The texture is akin to flan, but undeniably has all the French flair a Francophile could want. Most traditionally, cherries create the meaty fruit of clafoutis, but other berries and fruits, like raspberries, are also commonly used to pull off the recipe. While not necessarily a dessert, if you want to go in a savory direction, fruit can also be substituted for prosciutto, cheese, and tomatoes, so think of it like a choose-your-own-adventure type dish. No matter how you build it, though, clafoutis is one French creation that deserves more recognition, at least in the States.

#9803. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9802. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

#9801. Forget Butter Or Mayo: Spread This Rich Ingredient On Bread For Heartier Grilled Cheese

A grilled cheese is already plenty hearty, but the common tip of using cured meats to increase its satisfying flavor — like in this tasty maple bacon variation — may interfere with your filling's texture if you prefer a smooth, gooey filling. Duck fat is the perfect way around this because it adds meatiness without changing any other ingredients, enriching the bread with umami with just a single smear.

Duck fat is one of the most prized cooking fats in the culinary world because it has a higher smoke point than butter (around 375 degrees Fahrenheit) and a beautifully silky texture rich in subtle, meaty flavors. Just like spreading it on burger buns, using duck fat on grilled cheese can give you crispier bread because you can cook it at a higher temperature. When left at room temperature, it has a consistency similar to softened butter, making it easy to spread or drop in a pan, depending on your preference. Its unique composition of fats and subtle meaty flavor mean you'll notice its richness even in small amounts. Though it has a touch of gaminess, it's quite subtle and serves to elevate creamy and aged cheeses alike with an added layer of complexity.

Using duck fat on grilled cheese is pretty easy, but there are a few tricks that can really maximize your results. Blending it with another fat, using it for some added seasoning, and picking the right pan can all give you the perfect sandwich.

Mixing a fat with a high smoke point with one that burns more easily is a simple way to combine the best of both worlds. The richness of butter is irreplaceable, but you can incorporate some of duck fat's higher-heat cooking properties by swirling the two together before spreading the mix on your bread. Similarly, you can also bring your duck fat to a low, gentle simmer and add herbs and aromatics to flavor it beforehand. Whether you do this when rendering the fat yourself or just for a few minutes before adding your sandwich, a bit of sage can lend tremendous depth, while a smashed clove of garlic can mimic the rich flavor of toum.

While a nonstick pan is great for butter since it doesn't retain as much heat, you might want to go in the opposite direction for duck fat. A heavy cast iron or stainless steel skillet helps prevent the surface temperature from dropping when you add the sandwich, maintaining that lovely heat that makes duck fat work so well. Plus, animal fats are great for cast iron's seasoning, helping you maintain your pan's coating while you cook!

#9798. Add This Crunchy Ingredient To Ground Beef For Lighter Steakhouse Burgers (Hint: It's Not Breadcrumbs)

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The actual difference between a hamburger and a steakburger comes down to the quality of meat used in the grind, but the difference between a homemade steakburger and one from a steakhouse is all about a lighter texture. Melissa Clark, author of "The Big Book of Dinner: Recipes and Rules (and How to Break Them)," tells us that achieving that characteristic is quite easy if you use ground cracker crumbs.

"Any kind of cracker or breadcrumbs will make a burger lighter," Clark says. "Ritz and saltines work really well. They are very airy, which helps lighten the ground meat." Beef is rather dense, even if you avoid overworking it into a firm, puck-like consistency that's more similar to sausage than a tender patty. But a quarter cup of ground crackers per pound of meat can make a world of difference.

When meat cooks, it contracts and releases juice and fat. Crackers, however, absorb them rather than allowing them to seep out of the patty, preventing it from shriveling up too much. Since steakhouse burgers typically use thick patties, this also keeps them nice and moist. Whereas a thin sliver of well-crusted beef may be just what you want in a smashburger, retaining moisture is a vital component to keeping your steakhouse burgers not only light, but also at their peak flavor.

Using plain, unsalted crackers can still keep your steakhouse burgers light, but it would be a missed opportunity for better flavor. While you also don't want to use something starch-free, like a nut- or seed-based variety, Melissa Clark is a big believer in picking a tasty brand and smashing them up properly.

"Using crackers can add great flavor – Ritz, with their butteriness, are especially lovely," Clark explains. Flavorful but unobtrusive, Ritz crackers are the perfect addition to any savory dish because just about everything can benefit from their toasty richness. But if you want to get a bit experimental, you can also just as easily use Cheez-Its or anything seasoned. This is an easy way to avoid coming up with a specialty spice blend since you'll be adding enough to thoroughly flavor your meat.

Clark is also a proponent of using whatever method you can to grind the crackers into a fine powder. "Grind the crackers in a food processor, blender or tuck them in a plastic bag and crush them under a rolling pin," she added. Large chunks can make some bites unexpectedly soggy and, if using a seasoned cracker, a little too flavorful. Plus, if some parts of your blend don't have a starch, they may end up expressing their juices too much, leaving some bites juicy and light and others dense and dry.

#9797. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

#9796. Store-Bought Hummus Is 10x Better When You Add A Scoop Of This Condiment

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Among the most iconic Middle Eastern dishes, hummus blends chickpeas, tahini, olive oil, lemon juice, and optional seasonings to delicious effect. It's a dish that can be assembled at home, but many tasty store-bought versions are available, too. If your grocery store hummus happens to taste a little flat, though, reach for toum. Just a spoonful of this condiment will make a version that's 10 times better.

Hailing from Lebanon, toum is an emulsion made by blending a generous dose of garlic with oil, lemon juice, and sometimes water. Smooth and airy in texture yet with an underlying bite, it lends hummus a dose of garlicky goodness and acidity, readily transforming a bland flavor into a complex one. Plus, the condiment packs in extra fat, helping to improve the perceived creaminess of disappointingly dry hummus. Since toum is a homogeneous paste, it's easy to incorporate, and its flavor can be less aggressive than raw garlic, too.

You won't need much toum to make an impact. Start by mixing in just under a teaspoon per standard 8-ounce container, then work in gradual increments from there. For ease, grab a jar of toum online, or peruse the same grocery aisles where you bought the hummus. You could also easily prep your own toum in bulk — the condiment typically keeps for up to a month in the fridge.

A toum-inflected hummus makes a great dip, scooped up with za'atar-dusted pita chips, pretzels, veggie chips, or whatever other crisp your heart desires. Note that there are many other ways to use hummus in everyday cooking, though — especially when it's mixed with toum.

For example, consider topping the condiment with spiced ground beef or lamb, a popular Middle Eastern combination. Flavor the minced meat with earthy spices and fiery chilies, and the garlicky hummus makes for a mouthwatering flavor combo, turning the store-bought dip into an extra-hearty meal.

Alternatively, make the chickpea-based dip less of a centerpiece and use it as a sandwich spread instead — it would pair delectably with crunchy vegetables like cucumbers and onions, as well as greens like spinach. Served on whole-grain bread, the dip makes for a delicious vegetarian meal.

Looking for an extra creative twist? You could even use the toum hummus to make your next batch of tuna salad — the garlicky flavor will pair terrifically with the tinned fish. When you're craving Middle Eastern flavors but don't feel like cooking, keep the toum-hummus pairing in mind.
